Wednesday: Rebuild Your Question
Download the printable question rebuild worksheet (PDF)
This worksheet walks your own question through a slot structure, a rewrite, the three standards, and a partner test. It offers two structures and asks you to pick one:

Structure A for comparison questions, using population, intervention or exposure, comparison, and outcome.
Structure B for descriptive, exploratory, and process questions, using population or cases, phenomenon of interest, context, and evidence.

Most thesis questions in this college are not comparisons, so Structure B is the common case rather than the fallback.
Leave a slot empty if it is empty. The worksheet is built so an empty slot stays visible, because that is usually where the design problem is.

The partner test
The second half of the worksheet is the part to protect time for. Your partner asks what you would actually do to answer the question, and what in your proposal would change if the answer came back opposite to what you expect.
If nothing would change, the worksheet asks you to decide which of two things is true: the question is not really open, or the proposal is not really resting on it. Both are worth finding out in October rather than in November.

title: The Document
The Document
text:
Advisor-Ready, Week 12
This is the term most likely to be misread, so here is the standard plainly.
Advisor-ready does not mean finished, polished, or free of problems. It means a reader who is not you can follow the argument from question to method without you sitting beside them explaining what a section was supposed to say.
A draft is advisor-ready when:

every required section exists in some form, with no placeholder headings standing in for unwritten content;
the research question appears in the introduction, stated directly;
the literature review is organized around themes and supports the specific opening your question addresses;
the methods would let a reader judge whether the question can actually be answered;
figures, tables, and captions appropriate to the project are present, and each caption stands on its own;
the abstract is drafted; and
references are complete and Zotero-generated.

The Monday assembly and whole-document exchange test exactly this: whether the document reads without the writer explaining the missing connections. Do not send the advisor-ready version until the Week 12 release screen is complete.
Also bring a short conversation brief naming the document’s central argument, its strongest section, its most serious remaining problem, and your questions for me. Naming your own worst problem is not a confession. It is the fastest way to spend the twenty minutes well.

Whole-Document Review and Revision Memo
Before the release screen, exchange the complete draft with a peer. This is an integration check, not a third graded peer review. The reader traces one chain through the whole document:

What is the research question and why does it matter?
What does the literature establish, complicate, or leave unresolved?
How does the proposed method answer that exact question?
What outcomes would be distinguishable using that method?
What limits, feasibility constraints, or program requirements remain?

The writer submits a one-page revision memo naming the three most important changes made after that review, the evidence in the draft that prompted each change, and any issue that still requires expert judgment.


Week 12 Release Screen
Upload the advisor-ready document and required release materials to Canvas by Monday, Nov 23. The instructor uses the core rubric below for a bounded readiness screen during Week 12. Complete the required release revisions and send the document to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee no later than Wednesday, Nov 25. title: The Document
text:
Core Proposal and Thesis Rubric
Program-specific requirements may add criteria. They do not replace these course-level standards.



Table 2: Core final-document rubric.









Dimension
Satisfactory evidence




Question and significance
The research question is direct, bounded, and answerable; the document explains why the answer matters in its disciplinary context.


Literature synthesis and source use
Sources are relevant and traceable; the review organizes evidence around patterns, disagreements, limitations, and the opening for the project rather than one source at a time.


Question-method alignment
The unit or cases, evidence or data, collection or measurement, and analysis address the stated question. A reader can judge what the design can and cannot establish.


Feasibility, ethics, and alternatives
Applicable access, timing, equipment, permissions, safety, cost, ethics, and approval constraints are named. The document includes a defensible alternative for the largest design risk.


Expected or actual outcome logic
A proposal distinguishes plausible outcomes and explains what each would mean without inventing data. A thesis keeps claims within the actual results and analysis.


Limitations and calibrated claims
Consequential claims are supported and no stronger than their evidence. Important limits and unresolved decisions are visible.


Reader-facing structure
Sections form one argument from question through significance; transitions, headings, figures, tables, captions, and abstract help a reader follow it without the writer present.


Disciplinary and program fit
The document follows applicable disciplinary conventions and includes a completed requirements crosswalk confirmed with the Primary Advisor.


Accessibility and references
The document is readable in its submitted format; figures and tables have descriptive captions and non-color cues; citations and references are complete and consistent.






Every dimension must be satisfactory for milestone 15. A dimension rated not yet satisfactory is returned with the specific missing evidence and may be revised under the course resubmission policy when the institutional deadline allows it.

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
General Guidelines

As a Reviewer

Read the full document before writing any comments
Start with what works: identify specific strengths before addressing weaknesses
Be specific: “This paragraph is unclear” is unhelpful. “The transition between your literature review and your research question on page 3 is abrupt: consider adding a sentence that connects Theme X to your specific gap” is actionable.
Ask questions: “What would happen if…?” and “Have you considered…?” are more productive than “This is wrong.”
Focus on the work, not the person: “The methods section needs more detail” not “You didn’t write enough.”



As a Receiver

Read all feedback before reacting: your first instinct may be defensive; that’s normal
Separate the signal from the noise: not every suggestion needs to be adopted, but every suggestion deserves consideration
Ask for clarification if a comment is unclear
Document your response: in your process portfolio, note what feedback you incorporated, what you declined, and why

text:
Peer Review Worksheets
The stable worksheet criteria are published below, and paper copies will be available in class. Complete each review on paper and hand the worksheet and writer response to the instructor after the workshop. The result appears in the Canvas gradebook, but there is no routine Canvas upload. Each review requires you to point to evidence in the draft, explain why the issue matters, and name a priority. Three comments without that reasoning are not automatically three actionable suggestions.



Table 1: Peer review sequence and focus.





Review
Week
Focus




Week 9: Peer Review 1
9
Literature synthesis or thesis literature review: claims, evidence, synthesis, and organization


Week 11: Peer Review 2 and Professional Review Plan
11
Methods and expected results, or methods and actual results for Fall Graduation students: design, coherence, and support







Peer Review 1: Literature Synthesis

State the writer’s research question and literature-based rationale in your own words. Mark where the draft made each one visible.
Identify one paragraph that synthesizes multiple sources. Name the sources and explain what relationship the paragraph establishes among them.
Identify one place that remains source-by-source summary, or explain why you found none.
Test one consequential claim against its cited evidence. Is the wording no stronger than the evidence warrants?
Identify a disagreement, limitation, or boundary the draft handles well and one that needs more work.
Recommend the single highest-priority structural revision. Point to the relevant passage and explain what the revision would improve.



Peer Review 2: Question, Method, and Outcomes

Trace the argument chain: research question, evidence-based opening, proposed method, expected or actual result logic, and significance. Mark the first place the chain breaks or becomes hard to follow.
Test whether the unit, population, system, cases, or materials match the question.
Identify one missing design or analysis detail that would keep a reviewer from judging feasibility or answerability.
Check the applicable constraints: access, time, equipment, permissions, ethics, sample or case availability, and an alternative if the preferred design fails.
For a proposal, test whether at least two plausible outcomes can be distinguished using the proposed evidence. For a completed thesis, test whether the claims remain within the actual results.
Recommend the single highest-priority revision. Point to the relevant passage and explain why it comes before sentence-level editing.

After each review, the writer adds a short response naming one structural revision they will make, one recommendation they need to investigate, and one recommendation they will modify or decline with a reason. This response enters the process portfolio.

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
How Peer Review Is Evaluated
You are evaluated on the quality of the reviews you give, not on how well your own work is received:

Satisfactory: Every worksheet question is answered with evidence from the draft. The review identifies strengths and weaknesses, distinguishes a high-priority structural revision from minor editing, and explains why its recommendations would improve the question-evidence-method argument.
Not Yet Satisfactory: The review is generic, incomplete, unsupported by passages in the draft, or supplies edits without explaining their priority or purpose. It may be revised and resubmitted within one week.

title: Peer Review Guidelines
text:
Professional Review in Week 14
After the Week 12 release screen, send the revised proposal or thesis to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee. The Week 14 submission contains:

evidence that the document was sent and reviewed;
the comments, annotated draft, or meeting notes produced through the review;
a response memo explaining which major recommendations you will accept, modify, or decline; and
a prioritized revision plan for the applicable final deadline: Dec 14 for Fall Graduation students and Dec 16 for Proposal Development students.

You are evaluated on how you prepare for, document, and use professional feedback. Your grade does not depend on the reviewer’s writing style or the amount of feedback supplied.
A dated send record, your own summary of the substantive feedback, and your response are sufficient evidence. Redact personal contact information and anything unrelated to the project. Raw email threads and unredacted reviewer comments are optional and are not expected.

section: Writing Exercise 1 and the Topic Funnel
text:
Writing Exercise 1 and the Topic Funnel
Week 2, completed in class. Two pieces, both submitted together.
Open the accessible assignment page and printable worksheet. Milestone 2 also includes the separate Requirements and Outreach Workshop, due Wednesday. See the Foundations Milestones page for the combined standard.
The topic funnel takes your domain and narrows it in four steps: broad domain, focused problem, variable comparison, testable claim. We start on prompts I supply before anyone works on their own topic.
Step three often takes more than one attempt. That is productive work: a domain becomes a question when you can say what varies against what. Try a version, test it with a partner, and revise it. A claim that could turn out to be wrong gives you something you can genuinely investigate.
The diagnostic revision works on one paragraph from your Week 1 freewrite. That freewrite receives a participation result against an exploratory standard; polish is not part of that standard. Mark the claim, evidence, and reasoning you can find, and mark where a reader would need a part that is absent. Find the vague terms, the unsupported certainty, and the words doing no work. Revise without changing the meaning. Then explain which change improved it most, and why.
Keep the diagnostic revision on a separate sheet. The original freewrite is Milestone 1. The diagnostic revision and topic funnel together are Milestone 2, even though you hand in all three paper items at the end of Monday’s class.
Satisfactory means all four funnel steps attempted with a claim at step four that could be false, the paragraph revised, and the explanation naming a specific change rather than saying the writing is now clearer.

Identify one place that remains source-by-source summary, or explain why you found none.
Test one consequential claim against its cited evidence. Is the wording no stronger than the evidence warrants?
Identify a disagreement, limitation, or boundary the draft handles well and one that needs more work.
Recommend the single highest-priority structural revision. Point to the relevant passage and explain what the revision would improve.

Use line-number comments, not vague reactions. The point is to make the writer able to find the passage, judge the recommendation, and decide what to change.

title: Week 9: Peer Review 1
text:
Writer Response
After the review, add a short writer response naming:

one structural revision you will make;
one recommendation you need to investigate; and
one recommendation you will modify or decline, with a reason.

When you address a consequential comment, use one of three moves:

Accept: agree and make the change.
Decline with reason: disagree, and say what evidence or project logic supports that decision.
Need more information: identify what evidence, decision, or advisor input is still missing.

Reviewers can be helpful and still be wrong. The writer remains responsible for the document. The point is not to obey every comment. The point is to respond to each consequential one in a way another reader can follow.

Milestone 1 has two participation components because Labor Day leaves Week 1 with a single meeting:

Milestone 1 is complete when the survey has been submitted and the Freewrite meets the exploratory standard below. The survey is not a sixteenth milestone.
Open the accessible assignment sheet or download the printable PDF.

In-Class Davis Paper Intake
The paper intake is guided practice completed together during class. It is not submitted or graded. Keep the intake and your marked-up article as the first artifacts in your claims-and-evidence record.

Open the accessible Week 1 Literature Intake Form, which includes the two-page PDF for printing. Bring a printed copy if you prefer to have your own; copies will also be available in class.
Retrieve Davis (2010) through the University Libraries or another lawful source using the article DOI. Bring the paper in a format you can annotate.
Use the Reading Protocol as a starting procedure for locating the question, claim, evidence, and boundary.
See Week 1: Taking a Paper Apart Together for the class sequence and the distinction among these parts.

The form asks you to record candidate answers rather than an answer key. We will point to passages, compare interpretations, and revise the entry together.


Freewrite: What to Submit
Do not begin with a faculty directory. Begin by writing toward something you care enough to investigate.
Write informally about:

problems, systems, questions, or experiences that hold your attention;
why those interests matter to you;
what motivates you to investigate or work on them;
the kinds of activities or work you enjoy doing;
a role, job, profession, or career that might involve that kind of work;
what you already know and what you would need to explore; and
one uncertainty you want help thinking through.

This is exploratory writing. It does not need a settled thesis topic, a research question, faculty names, or polished prose. Its purpose is to give you material for the Week 2 topic-funnel exercise.
Format the freewrite as 1–2 pages in Times New Roman, 12 point, double spaced, with one-inch margins and continuous line numbers. Print it single sided. Bring it to class Monday, use it during the topic-funnel activity, and hand it in at the end of class. The result will appear in Canvas, but there is no routine Canvas upload. The literature intake form stays with you and is not part of the submission.


Satisfactory Standard
The freewrite is satisfactory when it:

responds specifically to the prompts rather than listing topics alone;
identifies at least one meaningful interest or motivation;
connects that interest to a possible kind of work, role, or future direction; and
names something you still need to explore or one uncertainty you want help thinking through.

Grammar, certainty, and having a settled topic are not evaluated.
The survey component is satisfactory when it is submitted. Survey answers are used for course planning, not evaluated as right or wrong.

Milestone 4: Primary Advisor Identification
Week 4, due Wednesday, September 30, on paper.
Use the printable Primary Advisor Identification form or Fall Graduation Literature and Reference Audit. The same page also provides the Search Workbook used during both Week 4 meetings.
This milestone asks you to name the faculty member who has agreed to serve as your Primary Advisor. The work leading to it is spread across three weeks: the Week 1 freewrite feeds the Week 2 topic funnel, you identify candidates and draft and peer-test one message in class, then complete the other two by Friday, September 18. Send all three messages no later than Monday, September 21.
That sequencing is deliberate. Sending happens early enough to preserve the Week 4 follow-up window. Bring copies of the sent messages and any replies to your Week 3 meeting so we can decide the next action.

What You Are Asking Someone To Do
Faculty say yes more readily when they know the size of the commitment. It is roughly seven touchpoints across the term, the largest being one 30-minute meeting in Weeks 2 to 4 and a document review around Dec 3 to 9. The full list is on the Advisor FAQ, which also contains a template letter you may send them.
Point them at that page. A request that comes with a clear scope is easier to accept than one that does not.


Satisfactory
The milestone is satisfied by naming a faculty member who has agreed, with:

their name, department, and the date they agreed;
how the agreement was made, meaning a meeting, an email reply, or a conversation you can point to; and
confirmation that they know the approximate December review window.



If No One Has Agreed by September 30
This is the one milestone that depends on whether another person replies to email, and a silent inbox is not a failure of your work. It is assessed on your professional communication, which is entirely within your control.
If no faculty member has agreed by Sep 30, hand in instead:

the three messages you sent, with the dates you sent them;
at least one follow-up, sent no sooner than five business days after the original and no later than Sep 28;
any replies received, including declines; and
a short note on what you will try next, naming at least one further candidate.

That submission is satisfactory. Then come see me. A stalled advisor search is usually a targeting problem or a timing problem, and both are fixable, but only if I know about it in September rather than October.






ImportantDo Not Wait Until September 30 To Tell Me



If all three of your candidates have declined by your Week 3 meeting, say so there. I can suggest faculty, and an introduction that comes from me lands differently than a cold email. The students who struggle here are not the ones whose first choices said no. They are the ones who waited.








NoteFall Graduation Track



Your Primary Advisor is already in place, so Week 4 asks for something else: a Literature and Reference Audit identifying missing sources, incomplete citations, unsupported background claims, and reference-library problems that must be resolved before the full thesis review.
Satisfactory means the audit names specific gaps with the sections they affect, rather than a general statement that the references need work.

title: Advisor FAQ
text:
What Is the Honors Thesis?
The University of Minnesota Honors Program requires students to complete a thesis as part of their honors requirements. The thesis:

Must be an original scholarly or creative work
Must be supervised by a UMN faculty member
Must be approved by the student’s honors committee
Requirements may vary by department: please check with your unit’s honors coordinator

The Honors Program’s own requirements document is posted here: Honors Requirements, University Honors Program (PDF).
Two committee rules are worth knowing before you agree to serve. The committee has at least three members, a primary advisor and two readers. At least one member must be tenured or tenure-track at the University, though not necessarily the primary advisor, and at least one member must be affiliated with the department in which the thesis is conducted. Non-tenure-track University instructors and researchers with relevant expertise may serve as readers; anyone outside the University requires a departmental petition approved by the Honors Program Director.

What If My Student’s Research Is Qualitative?
The course covers quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-methods approaches. Module 6 includes a dedicated qualitative track covering interview design, thematic analysis, and qualitative validity concepts. Your student’s proposal will be structured appropriately for their methodology.

title: Advisor FAQ
text:
What About AI Use?
AI instruction is not part of the CFAN 3091V curriculum, and the course does not use generative AI tools. No assignment requires or expects one. Work students submit must be their own thinking and their own words. The instructor may demonstrate a tool in class at her discretion; that does not authorize student use.
If your own lab or department has a different standard for AI use in thesis work, tell your student. Your requirements govern the thesis; this policy governs what happens in the course.

title: Syllabus: CFAN 3091V
text:
Course Description
You have a great research idea, now what? How do you turn your idea into a proposal? It has been said, paraphrasing Edison, that innovation is one percent inspiration, 99 percent perspiration. In this course, we will start with an inspiring idea and sweat our way to develop a research proposal.
Most students follow the Proposal Development Track and develop an original thesis proposal. Students graduating in Fall 2026 follow the accelerated Fall Graduation Thesis Completion Track and apply the same workshops to a complete honors thesis. You will learn to identify a research question, navigate University resources, write in the conventions of scientific communication, design or evaluate appropriate research methods, and produce the complete document required by your track.
Students will follow a step-by-step process that starts with choosing and defining a research idea, then proceeds through literature review and the development of a hypothesis, aims, objectives, and a research strategy. The course provides tools for understanding the structure of scientific reports and proposals, literature searches, and basic data interpretation. Students will learn about different research approaches and how to achieve consistency in their research projects. The course guides students in beginning and developing a written research proposal that will satisfy the requirements of their advisors, institution, and funding organizations.
The course is designed for students across all departments in CFANS. Whether your thesis involves field experiments in agronomy, sensory evaluation in food science, econometric models in applied economics, or qualitative interviews in natural resource management, the research process and writing skills taught here apply to your work.
This is a writing-intensive, workshop-style course. You will write every week. Your writing will improve through practice, feedback, and revision, not through a single high-stakes assignment at the end. The final Full Thesis Proposal or Final Thesis Draft is the culmination of a semester of scaffolded writing practice.

title: Syllabus: CFAN 3091V
text:
How This Class Runs
We work mainly at the board and on paper. I do not teach from slide decks. Instead, we build questions, arguments, outlines, and revisions together while the decisions are still visible. Bring paper and something to write with to every session, along with any handout or draft listed for that week.
That choice is deliberate. A finished presentation can hide the choices, false starts, and revisions that produced it. Here, we will make those moves visible: test an idea, notice where it fails, revise it, and explain why the revision is stronger. You will practice the same process in your own proposal work.
The board work is one part of the course record, not the whole of it. The course site provides the schedule, assignment criteria, readings, and materials you need to prepare and follow through. Canvas holds grades, private feedback, protected student records, and the assignments designated for online upload. If you need course materials in another format, contact me early so we can make a workable plan.
Week 4 is the exception. We work on screens that week, because library databases and Zotero are the subject of the lesson and the work requires live access. Bring a laptop for both sessions. You will build and document a search: record the terms you tried, what did not work, what you changed, and why you kept particular sources.

text:
Specifications Grading
This course uses specifications grading within the required A-F framework. The grade is determined by which bundle of milestones a student completes at a satisfactory standard, not by percentage weights. There are no points, no curve, and no percentage weights.
“Satisfactory” means the work contains every required part and meets the observable criteria on the relevant assignment page. Time spent or effort claimed does not substitute for those criteria. Instructor feedback on drafts is intended to support development and revision.



Table 2: Specifications-grading bundles.









Grade
Requirements




A
Complete all milestones at a satisfactory standard; earn a “strong” instructor-conversation rating; and submit a complete process portfolio


B
Complete all milestones at a satisfactory standard; earn a “satisfactory” instructor-conversation rating; and submit a substantially complete process portfolio


C
Complete at least 80 percent of milestones, meaning 12 of 15, at a satisfactory standard; satisfy the three essential document milestones; and submit a partially complete process portfolio


D
Complete at least 60 percent of milestones, meaning 9 of 15, at a satisfactory standard, including the three essential document milestones


F
Complete fewer than 60 percent of milestones, meaning fewer than 9 of 15, at a satisfactory standard






There are 15 milestones, one for each week of the term. Each course track has an equivalent 15-milestone sequence on the course schedule and assignments page. When a milestone has several parts, every part must be satisfactory for it to count. The process portfolio is named separately in the bundles above and is not among the 15.
Three milestones are essential for every passing grade: the Week 12 advisor-ready document and release screen, the Week 13 instructor conversation and professional-review submission, and the Week 15 final document. Milestone counts create room for an imperfect semester. They do not create a path around the complete proposal or thesis that the course exists to produce.

How the Week 13 Conversation Is Counted
The Week 13 conversation appears twice in the grading scheme. The two uses measure different things, and it is worth being explicit about which is which.
As milestone 13, it asks whether you did the work. You arrived with the advisor-ready document, you engaged with questions about design and evidence, and you completed the release revisions before sending the document to your Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee. Coming prepared and finishing those revisions satisfies milestone 13.
As a rating, it asks how the conversation itself went, judged strong, satisfactory, or needs development against the criteria on the Week 13 page. The rating is what separates the A and B bundles.
A rating of “needs development” does not by itself cost you milestone 13. Like any milestone rated not yet satisfactory, the rating can be re-earned: schedule a follow-up conversation within one week.


What Counts as a Complete Portfolio
The process portfolio has four phase sections, a mentor interaction log, and a final reflection. The bundles above use these three standards.



Table 3: Portfolio completeness standards used by the grading bundles.









Standard
Requirement




Complete
All four phase sections, the mentor interaction log, and the final reflection. Every artifact listed for a phase is present, and each phase explains at least one consequential decision.


Substantially complete
All four phase sections and the final reflection, with no more than two listed artifacts missing across the whole portfolio.


Partially complete
At least three of the four phase sections and the final reflection.






The course assigns straight A, B, C, D, or F grades. Plus and minus modifiers are not used.
The scaffolded assignment structure, regular progress reports, and three rounds of individual meetings exist to get you there. To support that, I offer Study Hall Hours, by appointment, where we review current assignments, work through writing and research questions, and take on common problems together.


How Much Feedback Each Submission Gets
Not everything you submit carries the same weight of instructor response.



Table 4: Feedback tiers by submission type.










Tier
Work
What you get back

Progress reports, primary-advisor identification, Professional Review Plan
I read them. No line-level feedback.


Scaffolded short writing

Brief feedback aimed at your next draft or action.


Substantive draft
Literature Synthesis Draft, Introduction, Literature Review, and Methods Draft
Detailed written feedback returned within seven calendar days and before the next dependent revision deadline. The Literature Synthesis Draft is returned by Nov 4; the Introduction, Literature Review, and Methods Draft is returned by Nov 18.

Peer Reviews 1 and 2
Assessed on the quality and specificity of the feedback you give, not the polish of what you submit.


Professional review

Assessed on preparation, communication, and use of feedback.


Final document
Full Thesis Proposal or Final Thesis Draft
Evaluated against the criteria for the student’s course track and applicable program requirements.








Progress Reports
Progress reports are the backbone of the early course. Proposal Development students submit Progress Reports 1, 2, and 3. Fall Graduation students submit two thesis progress reports. Reports connected to Weeks 3 and 7 serve as individual-meeting agendas. This is the same structure I use with my graduate students. You do not show up to a meeting empty-handed.
Each progress report uses a structured template:

What did you accomplish since the last report? Be specific: dates, meetings, hours.
What did you struggle with? How did you try to resolve it?
What is your plan for the next period? Name specific tasks and deadlines.
What questions do you have for me?

Progress means different things at different points in the semester. Early on it might mean identifying your domain and contacting potential mentors. Late in the semester it means drafting and revising thesis sections.
The Progress Reports page carries the full template, what counts as satisfactory at each stage, and the Professional Review Plan.


Writing Assignments
Writing assignments build progressively. Early ones are low-stakes exercises; later ones are thesis section drafts. Each includes specific criteria tied to that module’s objectives. Written feedback is provided on all of them.


Peer Reviews
There are two structured student peer review sessions, in Weeks 9 and 11. You review classmates’ writing using a structured protocol with specific criteria for each thesis section. Peer review is a core component of this course: structured feedback from a different reader catches what you cannot see in your own draft.


Professional Review
Week 14 is a professional review, not a third student peer review. Students send the released complete document to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee by Nov 25, after the Week 12 release screen and before the Week 13 instructor conversation. The reviewers should already have reserved the review window and should plan to return feedback around Dec 9. Students submit review evidence, a response memo, and a prioritized revision plan. The grade reflects preparation, communication, and use of feedback, not another person’s response speed.


Full Thesis Proposal (Course Assignment)
The Full Thesis Proposal is the substantial course document and the culmination of the semester’s work. It includes an abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, expected results, discussion/significance, conclusion, and references. It must meet both your department’s and the University Honors Program’s requirements.
Do not confuse this document with the UHP Thesis Proposal Form. The UHP form is a shorter administrative submission filed through the Honors Reporting Center. It asks for your thesis title, a brief prospectus, and your committee chair. It is not a substitute for the Full Thesis Proposal.
The Week 13 instructor conversation is about your developing Full Thesis Proposal or thesis; it is not the UHP filing deadline. For spring or summer graduates, the UHP Thesis Proposal Form is due December 1. Confirm the current date and any earlier department deadline with your advisor and departmental Honors Faculty Representative.


Final Thesis Draft (Fall Graduation Track)
Students graduating in Fall 2026 submit a complete thesis draft rather than a new proposal. They should already have filed the UHP Thesis Proposal Form, formed the Proposal Committee, and completed enough research to support thesis completion. Their final thesis and UHP Thesis Completion Form are due December 14, 2026. The Dec 16 course submission consists of the process portfolio and a record of the completion submission. Committee approval is due December 21 and remains an institutional decision rather than a course grade.


Resubmission
Any milestone rated “not yet satisfactory” may be revised and resubmitted once within one week. I will give you specific feedback on what needs to change.


Extra Credit
This course does not offer extra credit. Instead it is built with multiple pathways for improvement: low-stakes early writing that builds toward higher-stakes drafts, structured peer review that arrives before major submissions, progress reports that let you course-correct, and a resubmission policy on any milestone rated not yet satisfactory. The grading structure rewards consistency and growth rather than single high-stakes moments. You are never out of options.

Honors Thesis Requirements

University Honors Program Requirements
To graduate with Latin Honors you must complete an honors thesis in your major department. Your thesis must:

go beyond typical coursework, and cannot be a repurposed project from another course;
demonstrate your ability to synthesize existing work and present it succinctly;
show capacity to propose and execute a research idea within a timeline; and
produce writing at a publishable or public-presentation level of quality.

The full requirements document is posted on this site: Honors Requirements, University Honors Program (PDF). Read the thesis sections. Everything below summarizes that document, and where the two disagree, the Honors Program document governs.


Committee Composition
Your thesis committee has at least three members: a primary advisor and two readers. Two rules constrain who those people can be, and students routinely learn about the second one too late.

At least one member, though not necessarily your primary advisor, must be tenured or tenure-track faculty at the University of Minnesota.
At least one member must be affiliated with the department in which the thesis is conducted.

Beyond those two constraints, the remaining members may be tenured or tenure-track University faculty, or a non-tenure-track University instructor or researcher with specialized knowledge relevant to your topic. Members do not all have to come from the same program or college, and a committee that spans units is sometimes an advantage rather than a complication.
Anyone further afield, a community member, faculty at another institution, or an advanced graduate student, can serve only in rare cases, and only when your department petitions the Honors Program Director for approval. Do not assemble a committee assuming that route is open to you. If you need it, ask early.
Composition rules vary by department and may change. Confirm your committee structure with your department’s honors representative and against the current University Honors Program requirements before finalizing your committee.

Use of Generative AI
We do not use AI tools in this course. No assignment requires one, no assignment expects one, and you do not need one to do well here.
That is not a technophobic position. It is about what this particular course is for. You are learning to take a vague interest and turn it into a question someone could actually answer, then defend that reasoning in writing. Student Conduct Code
Students are expected to adhere to the Board of Regents Policy: Student Conduct Code. The University seeks an environment that promotes academic achievement and integrity, protects free inquiry, and serves the University’s educational mission. To support this environment, the University seeks a community that is free from violence, threats, and intimidation; that is respectful of the rights, opportunities, and welfare of students, faculty, staff, and guests; and that does not threaten the physical or mental health or safety of members of the University community.
The conduct code explicitly addresses disruptive classroom conduct, meaning behavior that substantially or repeatedly interrupts either the instructor’s ability to teach or a student’s ability to learn. The classroom extends to any setting where students work toward academic credit.


Use of Personal Electronic Devices
Classroom device policy falls under Teaching and Learning: Student Responsibilities. Using personal electronic devices in the classroom can hinder instruction and learning, for the student using the device and for others. The University establishes the right of each instructor to determine if and how personal electronic devices are used in the classroom.


Scholastic Dishonesty
Academic integrity standards are detailed in Teaching and Learning: Instructor and Unit Responsibilities. As students in a university community, you are expected to do your own academic work and to cite the sources of knowledge you draw on. Failing to do so is scholastic dishonesty, which includes plagiarism; cheating on assignments or examinations, including unauthorized use of online learning support and testing platforms; unauthorized collaboration, including posting student-generated coursework on platforms not approved for the course; taking, acquiring, or using course materials without faculty permission; submitting false or incomplete records of academic achievement; acting alone or with another to falsify records or dishonestly obtain grades, honors, awards, or professional endorsement; altering, forging, misrepresenting, or misusing a University academic record; or fabricating or falsifying data, research procedures, or data analysis.
When it is determined that a student has cheated, the student may be given an F for the course and may face additional sanctions from the University. The Office for Community Standards and the Center for Educational Innovation offer additional resources on academic integrity. Excused Absences and Makeup Work

Such circumstances include verified illness, participation in intercollegiate athletic events, subpoenas, jury duty, military service, bereavement, and religious observances. They do not include voting in local, state, or national elections.

Guidance is in Student Responsibilities. Taking notes is a means of recording information and, more importantly, of personally integrating and connecting it as part of your education. Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Equal Opportunity

The University provides equal access to and opportunity in its programs and facilities, without regard to race, color, creed, religion, national origin, gender, age, marital status, familial status, disability, public assistance status, membership or activity in a local commission created for the purpose of dealing with discrimination, veteran status, sexual orientation, gender identity, or gender expression.

title: Week 5: Research Questions and What Counts as an Answer
Week 5: Research Questions and What Counts as an Answer
text:
Purpose
Here is the failure I see most often in proposal drafts, and it is not a failure of effort. A student reads 20 papers, summarizes them accurately, and then writes a research question that none of those 20 papers would have changed. The reading happened. The inference did not move.
So this week runs on one question, and we will keep returning to it: does this knowledge actually change what you can conclude?
That question has teeth in both directions. A finding that contradicts your assumption should change your design, your question, or your expected result. A finding that confirms what you already believed should change how confidently you may assert it. If a source does neither, you have read it, but you have not used it. There is a difference between a fact that is interesting and a fact that is load-bearing, and a proposal that cannot tell them apart reads as a literature summary with a question stapled to the end.
You are not supposed to be good at this yet. Discerning which knowledge bears on an inference is a skill that takes practice, and it is the specific skill this week is built to develop.

title: Week 5: Research Questions and What Counts as an Answer
section: Monday: What Would Count as an Answer?
text:
Monday: What Would Count as an Answer?
Format: Focused instruction and a question-classification workshop.

Two Ways of Knowing
Research approaches are not ranked. They answer different questions, and they license different conclusions.



Table 1: What each approach can and cannot establish. The last row is the one that matters for your inferences.











Quantitative
Qualitative




The question sounds like
How much? How many? How often? Does X differ from Y?
How? Why? What is this like from the inside?


An answer looks like
A number, a rate, a difference, an interval
A pattern across cases, a process, an account of meaning


It can establish
Magnitude, frequency, and whether a difference is larger than the noise
Mechanism, context, and how people understand and act on something


It cannot establish, alone
Why the pattern exists, or what it means to the people in it
How common the pattern is, or how large the difference would be






Two misconceptions worth naming directly, because both show up every year. “Qualitative is not rigorous” is false. Rigor is a property of design and execution, not of whether the evidence is numeric. “Quantitative is always stronger” is also false. A precise number answering the wrong question is worth less than a careful account answering the right one.
We will go deeper into what statistical results can and cannot license in Week 6, and that is also where mixed-methods designs belong, because they make the most sense once you have seen where a single approach runs out.


Activity: Match the Question to the Approach
Most of Monday is this. I hand out the Match the Question to the Approach worksheet: twelve research questions from across this college, on paper, with no labels. Copies are provided in class, and the printable version is on the assignment page if you would rather arrive with one you have already read. The questions were written for this exercise rather than taken from anyone’s thesis, so you can be blunt about them. In pairs, sort them.

For each question, decide what the answer would have to look like. A number? A pattern across cases? An account of how something is experienced?
From that, name the approach the question requires.
Find the two questions you disagreed about most and write down why.
Rewrite one question so it would require the other approach. What had to change?
For that rewritten pair, name one conclusion the first version could support and the second could not.

Steps four and five are the ones that teach. A question is not quantitative or qualitative because of its topic. It is one or the other because of what would count as an answer. And when you change what would count as an answer, you change what you are entitled to conclude.


Discussion

What approach does your question require, and what would the answer look like?
Can anyone give a question that could be answered either way, and say how the two answers would differ in what they license?
Take your own question and answer this: what would have to change, either in the science or in what we currently know, before your conclusion would have to change? A new measurement? A result from a different system? An account from the people involved that contradicts the numbers? If you cannot name anything that would move you, the question is not yet doing work.

title: Week 5: Research Questions and What Counts as an Answer
text:
Wednesday: Refining the Question
Format: Workshop, on paper, with partner testing.
A vague question is not a modest question. It is a question that cannot fail, and a question that cannot fail cannot teach you anything. Refinement means adding enough structure that the question could come back with an answer you did not expect.






TipBreakout: What a Question That Cannot Fail Looks Like



Each of these is a real shape I see in Week 5 drafts. None of them is lazy. They are what a question looks like before it has been made specific.



Table 2: Six questions that cannot fail, and the specific thing missing from each.









The question
Why it cannot fail




Are cover crops good for water quality?
“Good” is undefined, so any result confirms it. No population, no comparison, no measure.


How does climate change affect agriculture?
True at every scale and in every direction. No answer could contradict it.


What are the benefits of local food systems?
The word “benefits” presupposes the finding. A study designed this way cannot return “none.”


Is organic farming sustainable?
Two contested terms and no criterion. The answer depends entirely on definitions you have not stated.


How do consumers perceive plant-based protein?
Which consumers, perceiving what, compared to what? Any collected opinion counts as an answer.


Does stress affect dairy cattle?
Almost certainly yes, at some magnitude, somewhere. The question has no edge to catch on.






Notice the pattern. Three of them fail because a key word is undefined, and three fail because they are true in advance. The repair is different in each case: define the term, or narrow the scope until a result could come back against you.



Structured Question Frameworks
A framework is a set of slots. Its value is not the acronym. Its value is that an empty slot is visible, and an empty slot is usually where the design problem is hiding.
The most familiar of these is PICO, which structures a question that compares one thing against another. It was developed for clinical questions about treatment, and it organizes a question around a patient or problem, an intervention or exposure, a comparison where one is relevant, and an outcome. Its stated value is procedural: filling the slots makes a question specific enough to guide which terms you search and where.
Two things about that are worth saying plainly, because you are being asked to use a tool built for a different discipline.
First, PICO comes from therapy-oriented clinical questions, and the review literature is explicit that it suits some information needs better than others (Eriksen and Frandsen 2018). It is not a universal template, and the next section is about what to do when it does not fit.
Second, whether PICO actually produces better searches than other structures, or than no structure at all, is not settled. A 2018 systematic review looking for evidence on exactly that question screened 2,163 records, assessed 22 full texts, and found only three eligible comparative studies. They varied so much in comparator, databases, and outcome measurement that no meta-analysis was possible, and the reviewers concluded that no solid practice implication could yet be drawn (Eriksen and Frandsen 2018). That is a statement about a thin evidence base, not a finding that PICO does not work.
So use it as what it is: a procedure for making an empty slot visible. That is a real and useful thing for a tool to do, and it does not require the tool to be proven superior. See the Evidence Boundary below for what this course does and does not claim about it.



Table 3: The four PICO slots and the design question each one forces.










Slot
What goes in it
The question it forces




Population
Who or what is studied, in what system and setting
Whose situation am I actually describing?


Intervention
The practice, exposure, treatment, or condition of interest
What exactly is being done or varied?


Comparison
What it is measured against, including current practice or no treatment
Compared to what?


Outcome
What is measured, in what units, over what period
How would I know it worked?






Worked example. Start with a question a student could plausibly bring to me in Week 5:

Are cover crops good for water quality?

That question cannot fail. Every slot is empty. Filling them:

Population: continuous corn systems on tile-drained fields in southern Minnesota
Intervention: a cereal rye cover crop interseeded into standing corn
Comparison: a cover crop drilled after grain harvest
Outcome: nitrate-nitrogen concentration in tile drainage, in mg/L, across one drainage season


In tile-drained continuous corn in southern Minnesota, does cereal rye interseeded into standing corn reduce nitrate-nitrogen concentration in tile drainage compared with post-harvest drilled rye, over a single drainage season?

The second version can be wrong (i.e., a question can fail), which is what makes it worth asking. It also tells you what to search, what to measure, and what evidence would count.


When PICO Does Not Fit
Most thesis questions in this college are not intervention comparisons, and forcing them into PICO produces a worse question rather than a better one. If your question is descriptive, exploratory, or about meaning and process, the comparison slot will stay stubbornly empty. That is information, not failure.






TipBreakout: Watching a Question Break the Template



Take a question that is perfectly good and entirely unsuited to PICO:

How do wildlife technicians decide what to do when a field protocol does not fit the conditions in front of them?

Now force it into the four slots:



Table 4: What happens when a process question is forced into the four PICO slots. Two slots resist, and the damage surfaces in the fourth.









Slot
What happens




Population
Fine. Wildlife technicians doing field data collection.


Intervention
Nothing is being administered. The closest thing is “encountering a protocol mismatch,” which is a situation, not an intervention.


Comparison
Empty, and not fixable. There is no control group of technicians who do not make judgment calls.


Outcome
You could force one, such as “number of protocol deviations.” But counting deviations answers a different question than the one you asked.






Two slots resist, and the damage shows up in the fourth. To fill Outcome you have to convert “how do they decide” into “how often do they deviate,” and that substitution quietly replaces a question about reasoning with a question about frequency. You would get a clean number and never learn what you wanted to know.
That is the tell. When filling a slot forces you to change what you are asking, stop filling slots and change the structure instead.
A related adaptation is worth knowing about, since some of you will work on exposures rather than interventions. In environmental, occupational, and public-health research, the same slot logic is adapted into PECO, replacing the intervention slot with an exposure (Morgan et al. 2018). That paper also makes the point this whole section rests on: no single framework is best everywhere, and the structure worth using depends on the kind of question being asked. If your question is about what a population is exposed to rather than what is done to it, that variant may sit closer to your work. Bring it to your Week 7 meeting if it applies.


Use the same discipline with slots that match your question:



Table 5: A slot structure for descriptive, exploratory, and process questions.









Slot
What goes in it




Population or cases
Who or what you are studying, and how those cases are bounded


Phenomenon of interest
The experience, process, practice, or decision you are examining


Context
The setting, system, place, and period that make the cases interpretable


Evidence
What you would collect that would count: accounts, observations, documents, records






Both tables do the same work. Name the parts, notice the empty slot, and ask what the emptiness costs you.


Activity: Rebuild Your Question
Use the Rebuild Your Question worksheet. Copies are provided in class. Keep it when we finish; the rebuilt question goes into Progress Report 2.

Write your current question at the top, exactly as you would say it out loud.
Fill the slots from whichever structure fits it. Leave empty what is empty.
Rewrite the question so it contains the filled slots.
Test it against three standards:

Is it answerable with evidence you could actually collect?
Is it specific enough to design a study around?
Is it significant? Who cares, and why?

Trade worksheets with a partner. Your partner asks two questions:

What would you actually do to answer this?
If the answer came back the opposite of what you expect, what in your proposal would change?


That second question is the inference test, and it is the one to sit with. It is the same test as the Monday discussion prompt, now aimed at your own proposal instead of someone else’s question.
Here is why it matters more than it looks. A proposal is an argument that some piece of work is worth doing, and the work is worth doing only if the result could land more than one way. So the test is not “is my question interesting?” It is “does my project have a stake in the answer?”
If nothing in your proposal would change, you are looking at one of two situations, and they need different repairs:

The question is not really open. You already believe the answer, and no plausible result would move you. The repair is to find the part you are genuinely uncertain about and ask that instead. It is often one layer down: not whether something works, but under what conditions, or for whom, or at what cost.
The proposal is not really resting on it. The question sits at the front of the document, but the methods, the design, and the expected results would proceed unchanged either way. The repair is structural. Either rebuild the design so it actually turns on the question, or admit the question you are really answering and write that one down.

Both are ordinary at this stage and both are cheap to repair in October. In November, when the document is drafted and your advisor is reading it, neither one is cheap. That is the whole reason this test happens now.


Whole-Class Share
We close by hearing a few questions before and after. Volunteering is genuinely optional, and a question that is still a mess is more useful to the room than a polished one, because the class gets to watch the repair happen rather than just admire the result.

Evidence Boundary
I ask you all term to say what your evidence supports and where it runs out, so it would be poor form not to do the same for the material I hand you.
Here is where this page stands.
What is supported. PICO’s four-part structure, its origin in clinical questions about treatment, and the point that its value is procedural rather than proven all come from a 2018 systematic review (Eriksen and Frandsen 2018). So does the harder statement: that review went looking for evidence that PICO improves search quality, found three eligible studies, judged them heterogeneous and at high or unclear risk of bias, and drew no practice implications. The PECO adaptation and the principle that no single framework fits every question come from a methodological framework paper in environmental health (Morgan et al. 2018), which is a commentary rather than a study that measured anything.
What is not. No source in this course’s evidence review shows that teaching a question framework improves student research questions, proposals, or theses. That is a different claim from the ones above, and nobody has established it for this setting. The non-comparative slot table in this section is my own adaptation for the kinds of questions students actually bring me. It is not taken from a validated instrument, and no study backs it.

Today we are studying the architecture of the Full Thesis Proposal, the substantial document you are writing for this course. This is different from the UHP Thesis Proposal Form, which is a short administrative submission containing a title, brief prospectus, and committee chair.

Proposal-map part
Davis worked example




Problem or context

Can a roller-crimper contribute to weed management in no-till soybean relative to chemical burndown and postemergence glyphosate regimes?

The study is positioned in the need for practical weed-management systems that reduce reliance on herbicides while keeping the crop viable.

Field comparison of cover-crop and burndown treatments, with weed biomass and soybean yield outcomes measured directly.

Evidence about whether roller-crimping can function as part of a workable weed-management system rather than as a theoretical alternative alone.

title: Week 6: Statistical Discernment and Mixed Methods
Week 6: Statistical Discernment and Mixed Methods
section: Monday: What a Result Does and Does Not License
text:
Monday: What a Result Does and Does Not License
Format: Focused instruction, then guided practice on a shared paper.
Statistical discernment begins before calculation. A result is interpretable only in relation to the question, design, population, measurement, and uncertainty that produced it.
That caution is not merely stylistic. Hill and colleagues (Hill et al. 2024) ran a randomized experiment in an introductory statistics course, giving students short written vignettes reporting a finding and asking how strongly they read it as causal. Both the wording of the finding and its topic affected their answers, and associational language by itself did not reliably prevent a causal reading. This study does not test our class activity, but it gives us a concrete reason to inspect the sentence and the study design together.

Probability, and What a P-Value Actually Is
You do not need to compute a p-value to read one, but you do need to know what it is a probability of, because that is where nearly every misreading starts.
Start with the picture, because the arithmetic follows from it.






Figure 1: Two expectations, one result. The shaded area is the p-value: how much of the no-effect curve sits at or beyond what you observed.



Both curves are expectations, not data. Each one says: if this were the true state of the world, here is the spread of results you would expect to see. The left curve assumes no effect. The right curve assumes a real one.
Now look at where the curves overlap, because that region is the entire problem. The observed result sits inside it. It is an unremarkable outcome under the right-hand curve and an unusual one under the left, but it is a possible outcome under both. No amount of arithmetic changes that.
The p-value measures one thing on this picture: the shaded area, meaning how much of the no-effect curve sits at or beyond your result. A small p-value says your data would be surprising if there were no effect. It does not say how much of the right-hand curve sits there, and it never tells you which curve you are actually standing in.






TipBreakout: What “Probability” Means Here, With One Die



Before p-values, settle what a probability is a statement about.
A probability is a statement about a setup, not about a result you already have. Take a fair six-sided die. The probability of rolling a 4 is one in six, or about 0.17. That number describes the die and the throw. It does not describe any particular roll, and the moment the die lands the probability is gone: it either is a 4 or it is not.
So probability runs one direction, from the setup to the outcome. Given this die, how often would I see this result?
Now roll three sixes in a row. If the die is fair, the chance of that is one in 216, about 0.005. That is a small number, and it is a p-value in miniature: if the fair-die assumption held, this run would be surprising.
Here is the step almost everyone takes and should not. That 0.005 is not the probability that the die is loaded. It cannot be, because we never asked how often loaded dice turn up in the first place. If every die in the room is fair, three sixes is just a rare evening. If half the dice are loaded, the same run means something else entirely. The rolls alone cannot tell you which room you are in.
That is the whole misreading, in a form you can hold in your hand. The p-value answers “how surprising are these data if the assumption held?” People hear it answer “how likely is the assumption?” Those are different questions, and the second one needs information the data do not contain.


A statistical model is a set of assumptions about how the data could have come about. A p-value is computed under such a model, including the assumption that there is no effect, otherwise known as the null hypothesis. It reports how unusual data like yours would be if those assumptions held. In the words of the American Statistical Association’s formal statement on the subject, “P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model” (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016).
Now the direction, which is the whole game. The p-value runs from the model to the data: given these assumptions, how surprising are these data? It does not run from the data back to the truth of the hypothesis. The ASA states this directly: p-values “do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone” (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016).






ImportantWhat the ASA Statement Says



In 2016 the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement on statistical significance and p-values, written for researchers and practitioners who are not primarily statisticians. It sets out six principles, in the statement’s own words (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016):

“P-values can indicate how incompatible the data are with a specified statistical model.”
“P-values do not measure the probability that the studied hypothesis is true, or the probability that the data were produced by random chance alone.”
“Scientific conclusions and business or policy decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold.”
“Proper inference requires full reporting and transparency.”
“A p-value, or statistical significance, does not measure the size of an effect or the importance of a result.”
“By itself, a p-value does not provide a good measure of evidence regarding a model or hypothesis.”

Read those carefully, because they are more limited than the arguments people build on top of them. The statement does not say p-values are invalid; principle one affirms a legitimate use. It does not propose a replacement threshold. It notes that some statisticians prefer other approaches, including estimation with intervals and Bayesian methods, while saying those “rely on further assumptions” rather than endorsing them as superior. And the ASA is careful that none of this is new: “Statisticians and others have been sounding the alarm about these matters for decades, to little avail.”
The conclusion is the sentence to carry into your own proposal: “No single index should substitute for scientific reasoning.”


Notice what principle five gives you. Significance and magnitude are different questions, and a paper can answer the first while leaving the second unaddressed. A yield difference of 0.2 Mg/ha can be highly significant with enough replication and still be too small for a grower to notice. Significance answers “is it distinguishable from noise?” Magnitude answers “does it matter?” You need both, and only one of them is usually printed in bold.


Selective Analysis and the Published Record
Principle four is the one with the sharpest edge for you as a reader. Proper inference “requires full reporting and transparency,” and the ASA names the practices that violate it: “data dredging, significance chasing, significance questing, selective inference.” Their consequence is stated plainly. Such practice “leads to a spurious excess of statistically significant results in the published literature and should be vigorously avoided” (Wasserstein and Lazar 2016).
Sit with that phrase, “a spurious excess in the published literature,” because it is a claim about the shelf you are building your source set from. The individual analyses can each look defensible while the visible record tilts.
Here is the mechanism. Any real analysis involves choices: which observations to exclude, which outcome to treat as primary, which covariates to include, when to stop collecting. Make those choices after seeing which ones produce a significant result, and you will find significance more often than the stated error rate implies. This does not require dishonesty. It requires only that the choices be made in the presence of the results.
What you can do about it as a reader is narrower than you might hope, and it is worth being honest about that. You cannot detect this from a single p-value; the number looks the same either way. What you can ask is whether the analysis plan was specified in advance, how many outcomes and comparisons were examined against how many were reported, whether the primary outcome in the methods is the one featured in the abstract, and whether the reported result stands alone or sits in a pattern the authors show you.


Claim-Inspection Protocol
For each result, ask:

What exactly is being claimed?
Who or what was studied?
What comparison produced the result?
What was measured, and how?
How much uncertainty surrounds the estimate, and what is that uncertainty a statement about?
Does the design support the conclusion?
Is the difference meaningful in the research context?

Questions five and seven are the ones the material above equips. Before this week, “how much uncertainty” was a box to tick. You can now say what the number in that box is a probability of, and question seven is the one no statistic answers for you.


Guided Practice
The rest of Monday stays on the Week 1 article. You already know this paper, which means you can spend the hour on the inspection instead of on orientation.
I bring three claims about the Davis results and put them on the board. They are my sentences, not the authors’, and they do not all hold up. Your job is to run the seven questions on each one and decide what the printed results actually entitle that sentence to say. We work the first as a class, you work the second in pairs, and we compare answers on the third.
Expect to disagree about question seven. Whether an effect is large enough to matter is not a statistical question, and two people reading the same table can reasonably land in different places. That is the point of doing it out loud.


Mixed Methods: Designing for What Neither Approach Settles
Recall from Week 5 that quantitative and qualitative work license different conclusions, and that each has a row in the table listing what it cannot establish alone. Now you have seen a concrete instance. A significant difference in tile nitrate tells you the magnitude of a change. It tells you nothing about why some growers adopted the practice and others did not, and a proposal that needs both is not served by choosing harder.
That is what a mixed-methods design is for. It is not “both, because more is better,” and two studies stapled together in one document is not a mixed-methods design. The defining feature is a connecting logic: a stated reason the two strands are in the same study, and a named point where they meet.
Three common connecting logics, as we will use the term in this course:

One strand explains the other. Measure the effect, then use interviews or cases to account for the variation the numbers show.
One strand builds the other. Use exploratory work to find out what the right questions and categories even are, then measure at scale.
The strands test the same claim from different angles. Where they agree, confidence rises. Where they disagree, that disagreement is a finding and belongs in the write-up rather than in a footnote.

The design question to answer in your Blueprint is not “should I do mixed methods.” It is: what does my question need that one strand cannot deliver, and where exactly do the strands meet? If you cannot name the meeting point, you have two studies and one deadline.

text:
Part 3: Taking One Paper Apart Together
Everyone works from the same paper. I will lead the dissection at the board, and we will complete the Week 1 Literature Intake Form together. The form page includes a two-page printable PDF, and printed copies will be available. Keep the handout and your marked-up paper. They are the first entries in the claims-and-evidence record you will build across the course.

Why Build a Claims Ledger?
A reference list tells you what you found. A claims ledger records what you may use from it, why the evidence supports that use, and where the limits are. Building the ledger while the paper is in front of you saves you from trying to reconstruct the authors’ reasoning weeks later. It also helps you:

locate the exact passage, result, figure, or table behind a statement;
distinguish an author’s evidence from your own interpretation;
compare claims that agree, conflict, or apply under different conditions;
notice where several papers repeat a claim without adding new evidence; and
draft literature-review paragraphs around patterns in the evidence rather than writing one summary per article.

The paper form is the first entry, not the required long-term technology. You can maintain the same structure in several ways:

In Zotero: Create a child note for a source with fixed headings such as Claim, Evidence and location, Connection, Boundary, and Status. Add a claim-ledger tag plus topic or method tags. When several sources address the same issue, shared tags let you retrieve them as a group.
In a spreadsheet: Use one row per claim, not one row per article. Useful columns include citation key, page or figure, claim, evidence, connection, limitation, topic, and status. One paper may therefore occupy several rows.
In a database: Import the spreadsheet as claim-source records connected to a source table by a stable source ID or Zotero citation key. A more developed system can keep separate source, claim, and evidence-link tables. That structure lets one source support several claims and one claim connect to evidence from several sources without duplicating the full citation.

For example, you might filter the ledger to find every claim tagged weed-management, group those entries by experimental design, and then compare which conclusions hold across sites. Or you might retrieve every entry marked needs closer reading before drafting so an uncertain interpretation does not quietly become a confident sentence. We will start on paper so the reasoning is visible; later, you may transfer the entries into the system that best supports your project.






NoteReading for this session



Davis, A. S. (2010). Cover-crop roller-crimper contributes to weed management in no-till soybean. Weed Science, 58(3), 300-309. https://doi.org/10.1614/WS-D-09-00040.1


This is a guided structural pass, not a test and not yet a critical appraisal. Published reading guides recommend reading with a purpose, previewing the article’s structure before reading closely, taking notes, and returning to the paper more than once. They also warn against treating the standard empirical article structure as universal: fields without conventional Methods and Results sections still have ways of gathering, analyzing, and interpreting evidence (Carey et al. 2020; George Mason University Libraries n.d.).
Our first pass adapts that guidance into four moves:

Preview. Inspect the title, abstract, headings, figures, and tables. Write down what you expect the paper to address, but treat that expectation as provisional.
Orient. Locate the problem or gap and state the research question in your own words. Point to the passage that supports your interpretation.
Trace. Select one consequential claim, then trace it to a specific result, observation, figure, table, passage, or other evidence. Inspect the method that produced that evidence.
Bound. Name what the selected evidence does not establish and what you would inspect on a closer reading.

We will record candidate answers, point to where they appear, and name what we are still uncertain about. “Candidate” matters. A first reading can produce a plausible interpretation that changes when we inspect the paper more closely.
The reading protocol gives you a starting procedure for empirical research articles. It is a heuristic, not a universal map. Different disciplines organize questions and evidence differently, and we will adapt the procedure as those differences appear.
