Week 8: Subject Mastery and Evidence Synthesis
section: Monday: From Source Notes to a Literature Structure
text:
Monday: From Source Notes to a Literature Structure

What a Literature Review Is Actually Doing
A literature review is not a sequence of article summaries. It is an argument about what is known, how it is known, where findings converge, and what remains uncertain.
The way that argument fails is specific, and I see it every year. A draft arrives where each paragraph handles one paper: what it studied, what it found, new paragraph, next paper. Every sentence in it is true. Nothing is connected. The reader finishes knowing what six papers said and still not knowing what the writer thinks the field knows. Then the objectives appear on the next page, as though they had been waiting there all along, attached to nothing.
You are not the first person to write that draft. Cisco, describing three years of writing-center work with students across disciplines, reports the same pattern: students “typically write a series of unrelated paragraphs, each of which summarizes one of the works reviewed rather than an integrative analysis of all the sources” (Cisco 2014). Boote and Beile, after reviewing dissertations at three universities, argue that students get very little formal training in how to analyze and synthesize a research literature, and that the quality of the reviews reflects it (Boote and Beile 2005). This is a skill nobody taught you. That is what this week is for.

Three Moves, in Order
Swales studied how published research introductions actually work and named the structure they share. He called it Create A Research Space, and it runs in three moves (Swales 1990):

Establish the territory. What is known, and why the area matters. This is the move students find easiest and routinely overdo.
Establish the niche. Where the known runs out. A disagreement, an untested population, a mechanism nobody has measured in your system, a claim that does not transfer. This is the move that gets skipped.
Occupy the niche. Your question, objectives, and hypotheses, arriving as the answer to the problem you just established.

Move two is load-bearing. Skip it and move three has nothing to stand on, which is exactly why objectives that appear out of nowhere read as arbitrary. They are arbitrary. The writing never made the case that anything needed doing.
Your thesis proposal makes the same three moves your sources do. The difference is that they had a whole introduction to do it in and you have a literature review, so the joins have to be visible.


Link Back to the Lit
That phrase goes in your margins more than any other thing I write. It means: you have asserted something, and you have not shown me where it came from or what it is doing for your argument.
Every sentence in a literature review does one of four jobs. You should be able to say which:

reports what a source found, in language no stronger than its design supports;
puts two or more sources in relation: agreeing, disagreeing, measuring different things, or studying different populations;
states what that relation means for your question; or
names what the relation leaves unsettled.

A paragraph built only from the first job is a summary. A review built only from summaries is a book report with citations attached. Diagnose your own draft by labeling each sentence with the job it does. If nearly all of them are the first job, that is a finding about the draft, and it is fixable.


A Gap Is Not an Absence
The gap you name is the hinge between the literature and your objectives, and it is where drafts most often break. “No one has studied this” is almost never true, and it is the easiest sentence in your proposal for a committee member to disprove. What you are claiming is narrower and stronger: these studies address this question in these systems, and the thing I want to know sits outside where their evidence reaches.
How much literature you must cover to say that honestly is genuinely contested. Boote and Beile argue for comprehensiveness, treating the review as the foundation the research stands on (Boote and Beile 2005). Maxwell, replying in the same journal, argues that a review should be judged on relevance to the research being proposed, and that it is a component of the research rather than the ground under it (Maxwell 2006). For a one-semester honors thesis, Maxwell describes the achievable target. You are not going to be comprehensive. You are going to be relevant, and you are going to state what your search boundary was so a reader can see the edge of your claim.


When Have You Read Enough?
You will ask me this, most of you around now, and counting will not answer it. One could argue that fifteen relevant sources can beat forty sources you have filed. So here is the test I actually use, and we will spend ten minutes at the board on it today.
Draw the paper you have not written yet. Not an outline. The manuscript, in its published form, empty:

Table 1. Your weather data, or your method timeline. Whatever your field puts first to let a reader judge the conditions the study ran under.
Table 2. Your model statistics. This one matters more than students expect. If you cannot say what model your design implies, or what its table would have to contain, then you do not yet know how your own question gets answered.
Figure 1. Your first response variable, with your treatments on it. Then the part that does the real work: rank the treatments. Put them in the order you expect, from what you know about the system, and be ready to say why that order and not another one.
Every remaining table and figure, the same way.

Then write the abstract. Then write the conclusion.
You are done reading when you can do that and defend it.
Notice what the ranking is doing. Everything before it can be produced by someone who has read carefully and understood nothing. An axis label is a fact about your design. The order of the bars is a claim about your system, and it can come from nowhere except what you have read and what you have reasoned from it. Rank the treatments and defend the order, and you have synthesized the literature. Fail to, and you have consumed it. Those are different things, and the board will tell you which one you did.
The test also fails better than “I have not read enough,” because it tells you where. A ranking you cannot defend points at one specific mechanism you do not understand yet, and that is a search you can go run this week rather than a vague instruction to read more.
If your project is not an experiment with treatments, the move is identical and the objects change. Draw the table of cases or sources and what varies across them. Draw the figure, matrix, or map that would display the pattern you expect. Draw the sequence your account will follow. Then commit: which cases you expect to resemble each other, which explanation you expect to dominate, which period you expect the shift to show up in. Same demand. Predict the shape, then defend the prediction from what you have read.
You will do this properly later. Week 11 drafts a real expected-results section with two outcomes, one for the hypothesis holding and one for it failing, and Week 12 works on the figures themselves. This week it is a diagnostic, not a deliverable. Chalk and ten minutes.






NoteFall Graduation Track: Run It Backwards



You already have the real tables and figures. Cover the results, then rank the treatments as you would have predicted them from the literature alone, and uncover. Where your prediction and your result diverge is where your discussion section already has something to say, and it is usually the most interesting paragraph in the thesis.





Reading Clinic: Where Do These Papers Disagree?
Fifteen minutes, and it closes a thread that has run since the first week. Each reading clinic has asked a different question, and until today the unit has always been one paper:



Table 1: How the reading clinic has built across the term.





Week
The unit
The question it asked




1
One paper
What does it say?


4
One paper
Where did it get that?


6
One paper
Was it entitled to say it?


8
Three papers
Where do they fail to agree?






The unit changing is the whole point. Lay three papers side by side, your Week 1 article and two of your own, and find one place where they do not agree: a different finding, a different population, a different definition of the same term, a limitation one names and the others pass over.
Disagreement is what the matrix below is built to hold. If three papers in your area agree about everything, you are either reading too narrowly or you have not read them closely enough.


Synthesis-Matrix Activity
After a short model, most of Monday is work time. Build the matrix in class so questions about categories, conflicting findings, and thin source notes can be resolved while the evidence is still in front of you.
Start from your Week 5 Search Record. Before building a single row, write a two-sentence source-set rationale: what question this set of sources can answer, and what your search boundaries mean it cannot represent. That second sentence is what makes your later gap claim defensible rather than absolute.
Then build one row per retained source. The columns are not arbitrary, and they are not new. They are the Week 5 slots turned sideways. PICO and the non-comparative slot structure made you name the parts of your own question; the matrix asks the same of every paper you kept, so the parts line up in columns and the differences become visible.



Table 2: Where each matrix column comes from.









Matrix column
The Week 5 slot it comes from




Research question
The question as a whole


Population or system
Population, or population and context


Method
Intervention and comparison, or phenomenon and evidence


Principal finding
Outcome


Limitation
Usually the slot the paper left empty


Relevance to your project
Whether its slots match yours


Relationship to other sources
The comparison the columns now make possible






Two papers that fill the same slots differently are not disagreeing. They are answering different questions, and the matrix is what lets you see that before you write a sentence claiming they conflict.
Use the completed matrix to identify two or three themes that can organize your review. Boote and Beile’s central argument is that this analytic work, not the collecting, is the part that makes someone a scholar of their area (Boote and Beile 2005).


Matrix Decision Rules
Use the same rules for every row:

Record the paper’s claim in language no stronger than its design permits.
Separate a different result from a different population, measure, definition, or method. Those are not interchangeable disagreements.
Mark “not reported” when the paper does not answer a matrix question. Do not infer an answer to make the row look complete.
Put sources in the same theme only when you can name the shared question or concept.
Treat a gap as bounded by the Search Record. “I did not find” is not the same claim as “no research exists.”







TipBreakout: One Row, on a Paper Everyone Has



Work in pairs for ten minutes. Before you build rows from your own sources, build one from Davis (2010), because everyone in the room has read it and nobody has to spend the time orienting.
Fill these cells together, out loud:



Table 3: A worked matrix row.









Column
Davis (2010)




Population or system
No-till soybean following cereal rye


Method
Roller-crimper compared with chemical burndown, across cover crops and postemergence glyphosate rates


Principal finding
Following cereal rye, the rolled system left 56% less surviving weed biomass than the burndown system


Limitation
Weed-interference yield loss did not differ by termination method under the study conditions






Now run the rules on what you just wrote.
Rule 1. “Roller-crimping controls weeds” is stronger than the design permits. The row says what was compared, following which cover crop, and by how much. Keep the comparison in the sentence or the claim floats free.
Rule 3. Some of your cells will be empty, and empty is a finding. Write “not reported” rather than inferring a plausible value, because in a month you will not remember which cells you filled from the paper and which you filled from yourself.
Rule 2, the one that matters most this week. Suppose your second source reports that roller-crimping did not suppress weeds. Before you write that the two papers disagree, check the columns. Different cover crop? Different region or planting date? Weed biomass measured, or weed density counted? If the slots differ, you have two papers answering different questions, and writing them up as a conflict is an error your committee will find.
Rule 5. If nobody has run this comparison in your system, your sentence is “within the boundaries of the search recorded in my Search Record, I did not locate studies in system B,” not “no one has studied system B.”

We will not meet on Oct 28 because I am out of the office. The work does not disappear. Monday’s model, your synthesis matrix, and the paragraph shell below give you the structure for an independent drafting session.
Complete these steps:

Draft one paragraph that states a pattern across multiple sources, identifies an important difference or limitation, explains why it matters for your question, and stays within the reviewed evidence.
Diagnose the paragraph yourself, using the four jobs above. Label the sentence that states the cross-source relationship, mark every sentence that discusses only one source, and identify the phrase that bounds the gap. If there is no cross-source sentence, you have written a summary.
Revise the paragraph, then integrate it into the Literature Synthesis Draft. Save the original and revised versions for your process portfolio.

Paragraph Shell
Use this shell when the relationship among sources is still hard to state. Replace every bracketed prompt with language supported by the sources in front of you:

Across [source set], the evidence converges on [bounded pattern]. The sources differ in [finding, population, definition, measure, or method], with [source or group] showing [supported result] and [source or group] showing [supported contrast]. That difference matters for this project because [consequence for the question or design]. Within the limits of [search and source-set boundary], the unresolved issue is [bounded uncertainty], which this project addresses by [specific question or design move].

Read the shell against the three moves. The first two sentences establish the territory, the third and fourth establish the niche, and the last clause begins to occupy it. That is the same structure your sources use, compressed into one paragraph so you can practice it before it has to carry a whole section.
This is a structure for reasoning, not language to submit with prompts still in place. If the matrix does not support one of the sentences, narrow the sentence or return to the sources.

title: Week 8: Subject Mastery and Evidence Synthesis
text:
Evidence Boundary
The source-set protocol, the matrix columns and decision rules, the four jobs a sentence can do, the read-enough test, and the paragraph shell are course procedures. They come from how this thesis work is supervised, not from a study showing they teach synthesis better than something else would.
The read-enough test is the instructor’s own supervision practice, offered as instructor judgment and labeled as such. No source in this course’s evidence review supports a claim that sketching expected tables and ranking treatments improves student synthesis. It is used here because it produces a specific, checkable failure instead of an unmeasurable one, which is a claim about the test’s structure rather than about its measured effect.
Four published sources are cited above, and each is doing a bounded job:

Cisco (2014) is a practice account from a university writing center, reflecting on one political science course. It is offered as a description of the failure pattern, not as evidence that any teaching method fixes it (Cisco 2014).
Boote and Beile (2005) studied dissertation literature reviews at three universities. Their subject is doctoral education, so their findings describe a population older and further along than this class (Boote and Beile 2005).
Maxwell (2006) is a published commentary disagreeing with them about what a review is for. It is included because the disagreement is real and this page takes his side for a one-semester thesis, not because it settles the question (Maxwell 2006).
Swales (1990) is a foundational work of genre analysis describing how published introductions are structured. It supports the claim that the three moves exist in the literature, not a claim that teaching them improves student writing (Swales 1990).

All four are prose attribution. The course evidence review has not verified a source for claims about teaching synthesis across disagreeing texts or teaching bounded gap identification, so none of these is presented as verified lecture evidence, and the Week 8 lecture-evidence records carry the outstanding review as a required action on both sessions.

Learning Objectives
By the end of this week, you should be able to:

distinguish expected results, which a proposal projects, from actual results, which a completed study reports;
write an expected results section that follows from your methods and literature rather than from what you hope to find;
draft a discussion connecting those expected findings to the literature and to their limitations; and
give substantive peer review on another writer’s methods and expected results.







ImportantKey Distinction



Previous semesters identified confusion between “expected results” (what you anticipate finding, based on logic and literature) and “actual results” (what you found, based on data). This module focuses exclusively on expected results: the kind you write for a proposal before data collection begins.

Minutes
What we do




About 12
Distinguish expected results from actual results and connect outcomes to the method


About 15
Model one hypothesis-to-prediction-to-outcome chain


About 25
Complete the two outcome sketches and the distinguishing-evidence check


About 13

About 10

Topics

What “expected results” means in a proposal: projecting plausible outcomes, not making things up
The logic chain: hypothesis → prediction → expected outcome
What outcomes does your literature review suggest are likely?
What patterns do similar studies report?
Plausible alternatives: Expected result A if hypothesis holds; expected result B if it does not
Tables of anticipated findings: what would the data look like?
Writing the discussion: connecting findings to existing literature, acknowledging limitations, articulating significance, identifying future directions



Activity: The Two-Outcome Table
Most of Monday is drafting. Use the Two-Outcome Table worksheet, one row for the outcome if the hypothesis is supported and one for the outcome if it is not supported.

Write your hypothesis in one sentence.
Write the prediction that follows from it, in the units you would actually measure.
Draw the table or figure you would expect if the hypothesis holds. Axes, units, and rough magnitudes. It does not need to be neat.
Draw the second one: what the same table or figure looks like if the hypothesis does not hold.
Write one sentence for each explaining what a reader should conclude.

Then trade with a partner and answer one question about their pair of sketches: could you tell these two outcomes apart if you saw the real data? If not, the prediction is not yet specific enough to be worth testing.


Discussion

For your study, what would it mean if your hypothesis is wrong? Is that a useful result?
How do you write about expected results without sounding like you are fabricating data?

title: Week 12: Figures, Tables, and Abstracts
Week 12: Figures, Tables, and Abstracts
text:
Monday: Figures, Tables, and Abstracts
Format: Short clinics + proposal assembly workshop

Topics

General principles: clarity, consistency, accuracy, simplicity
Figure types and when to use each:

Bar charts, scatter plots, box plots for quantitative data
Conceptual diagrams, flow charts for frameworks and processes
Maps for spatial research

Table structure: row headers, column headers, alignment, units, meaningful ordering
Writing table captions and figure legends: descriptive, self-contained, and concise enough that a reader can interpret the visual without searching the body text
Common mistakes: distorted or truncated scales, 3-D effects, dual axes that invite false comparisons, rainbow color scales, missing units or denominators, unexplained abbreviations, excessive precision, chartjunk, and repeating the same information in prose and a visual
Tools: R/ggplot2, Excel, BioRender (for conceptual diagrams), draw.io (for flowcharts)
Abstract structure: context → gap → objective → methods → expected contribution (250–300 words)



Examples
We will compare published examples of effective and misleading visual design. The point is not to mock a graphic; it is to identify the decision that makes the visual harder to interpret. We will use this discussion of truncated axes, this statistical-figure reporting guidance, and these caption examples.


The Stand-Alone Test
“Stand alone” does not mean that a figure or table needs no connection to the argument. It means that a reader who encounters the visual apart from the paragraph that first introduced it can still determine what was measured or shown, for whom or what, under what conditions, and how to read every label, symbol, abbreviation, and uncertainty mark. The visual should add information; the prose should explain why that information matters.
Use this test: cover the surrounding paragraphs and ask, What is this, who or what does it describe, what do the numbers or marks mean, and what comparison should I make? If the reader cannot answer, repair the visual or its caption/legend before polishing the prose.


Caption and Legend Recipe
The table caption goes above the table. The figure legend goes below the figure. Both begin with a number and a specific title, not a vague label such as “Results.” Then include the information needed to interpret the object:

What: the variable, relationship, process, or comparison shown.
Who or what: the population, system, cases, samples, or documents.
How: the design, time point, grouping, or calculation that produced it.
How to read it: units, denominators, symbols, colors, line types, abbreviations, and uncertainty or statistical notation.
Source and boundary: the data source, adaptation credit, and any limit that changes what the reader may conclude.

Example table caption: Table 1. Mean soybean yield and weed biomass by treatment in the field comparison. Values are means across four plots per treatment; yield is reported in Mg ha−1 and weed biomass in g m−2. Error bars are not applicable because this table reports means only. Adapted from the study protocol described in the methods.
Example figure legend: Figure 1. Expected relationship between cover-crop biomass and soybean yield under the proposed field comparison. Each point represents one plot; the horizontal axis is cover-crop biomass (g m−2), and the vertical axis is soybean yield (Mg ha−1). The shaded band marks the range of outcomes the proposal treats as practically acceptable, not a confidence interval.
Do not put a conclusion in place of a description. The caption tells the reader what the visual contains and how to interpret it; the paragraph tells the reader what the pattern means for the research question.


A Short ggplot2 Clinic
Use ggplot2 only if it serves your project. This is a 15-minute reproducible plotting clinic, not a programming unit. The transferable sequence is data → mapping → geometry → scales → labels → caption:
ggplot(data, aes(x = treatment, y = outcome, colour = group)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Treatment",
    y = "Outcome (units)",
    colour = "Group",
    caption = "Source: ...; points represent ..."
  ) +
  theme_classic()
Students using Excel or another tool apply the same checks: map the correct variables, label the full variable names and units, use a legend only when it decodes information, and record the source and uncertainty. The official ggplot2 labels documentation and guide documentation are references for labels and legends, not required reading.


Assembly Begins Monday
The clinics are short on purpose. The second half of Monday starts the assembly: put your sections in order, read the seams between them, and list what is missing. Wednesday finishes that work and tests it on a partner.
Starting Monday matters because the gaps you find are usually not sentence problems. They are a missing method detail or a claim with no source behind it, and those take more than one session to close.


Whole-Document Review and Release Screen
Format: Workshop
Upload the complete working Advisor-ready Full Thesis Proposal and required release materials to Canvas before class on Monday, Nov 23. This is the draft you submit for the instructor’s full-document review. The exchange below is an informal whole-document critique, not one of the two graded student peer reviews. Peer Review 2 happened in Week 11. The purpose today is to test whether the document works as one readable argument without the writer supplying missing connections.
Your working draft should incorporate the highest-priority Peer Review 2 edits you can complete in the available time. It may still contain unresolved comments; identify those decisions in the Whole-Document Revision Memo. The instructor review focuses on the complete argument and the three revisions that matter most, not line-level editing of every sentence.

Use the Visual Audit and Caption Clinic worksheet. For each visual, answer:

Is it necessary, and does it add information beyond the text?
Can a reader identify the population, variables, units, denominators, and comparison without the surrounding prose?

title: Week 2: Technical Writing and Thesis Requirements
Week 2: Technical Writing and Thesis Requirements
text:
Monday: Technical Writing Fundamentals
Technical writing helps another reader inspect your reasoning. The goal is not to sound complicated. The goal is to make the relationship among the question, evidence, method, and conclusion visible.

Topic Funnel
Your Interest, Motivation, and Direction Freewrite, shortened here to the Freewrite, may contain several interests, a possible direction, or only the beginning of a question. Progress Report 1 asks you to name a domain and say a rough research question out loud. This drill covers that distance in four steps.

Broad domain. Write the area you care about in one phrase.
Focused problem. Name one thing inside it that is unknown, contested, or going wrong.
Variable comparison. Name what you would compare against what.
Testable claim. Write one sentence that could turn out to be wrong.

The Davis paper from Week 1 gives us a complete worked example:



Table 1: A worked topic funnel based on Davis (2010).









Funnel step
Davis example




Broad domain
Weed management in no-till soybean


Focused problem
Can a roller-crimper help suppress weeds with less reliance on herbicides without increasing soybean yield loss?


Comparison
Roller-crimper versus chemical burndown, across cover crops and postemergence glyphosate rates


Testable claim
In no-till soybean following cereal rye, roller-crimping will reduce surviving weed biomass without greater weed-interference yield loss than chemical burndown.






Then choose one of these practice domains with a partner: calf health, food storage, pollinator habitat, household adoption of energy upgrades, music practice, or historical newspaper coverage. These are starting points, not facts. Your job is to supply a focused problem, a comparison, and a claim that could be checked.
For an experimental or observational question, try this sentence frame:

In [population or system], [outcome] will [increase, decrease, or differ] under [condition or exposure] compared with [reference condition].

Not every thesis is an experiment. For a qualitative, historical, or interpretive project, the comparison may involve cases, time periods, texts, groups, or competing explanations:

Across [cases or sources], [pattern or interpretation] will be more evident under [condition, period, or context] than under [comparison].

Expect the first few attempts to stall at step three. That is the hard step. A topic becomes investigable when you can name the difference, relationship, pattern, or interpretation you will examine. The funnel is a starting structure, not a demand that every field use the same kind of hypothesis.


Informal Notes and Technical Prose
Informal writing records what you are noticing. Technical prose lets another reader inspect exactly what you mean and how far the evidence reaches. The difference is not bigger words.



Table 2: Moving from informal notes to inspectable technical prose using Davis (2010).










Informal note
Technical revision
What changed




The roller-crimper worked really well.
In plots following cereal rye, the rolled system left 56% less surviving weed biomass than the burndown system.
“Worked” became a named outcome, comparison, and quantity.


It did not hurt the soybeans.
Under the study conditions, weed-interference yield loss following cereal rye did not differ by termination method.
The revision names the measured outcome and limits the claim to the study conditions.


This proves farmers can stop spraying.
The study tested whether glyphosate rates could be reduced under specific cover-crop and termination treatments; it does not establish that herbicides can be eliminated in every system.
The revision replaces unsupported certainty with the boundary of the evidence.






Use three questions when you revise: What exactly happened? Compared with what? Under which conditions?


Diagnostic Revision
Use one paragraph from the Freewrite. That assignment earns a Satisfactory or Not Yet Satisfactory participation result against its exploratory standard. Grammar, certainty, and polish are not part of that standard. Here, you are using a paragraph you already wrote to see what changes when a reader needs to inspect the reasoning.

Select one paragraph from the Freewrite.
Mark its main claim, evidence, and reasoning. If one is absent, mark the place where a reader would need it.
Identify vague terms, unsupported certainty, and unnecessary wording.
Revise the paragraph without changing its meaning.
Explain which revision most improved the paragraph and why.

Complete the topic funnel and diagnostic revision on the Week 2 Writing Workshop worksheet. You will submit both as the Monday parts of Milestone 2. Submit the original Freewrite separately as Milestone 1 at the same time.

Wednesday: Thesis Requirements
Proposal requirements vary across programs. You are responsible for finding the requirements that apply to your degree and confirming them with the appropriate program contact.

Read them before class. Two rules catch people out: at least one committee member must be tenured or tenure-track at the University, and at least one must be affiliated with the department where the thesis is conducted. Those can be the same person, but often are not.

Requirements Audit
Keep two deliverables separate in your notes:

Full Thesis Proposal: the substantial document developed in this course.
UHP Thesis Proposal Form: the shorter administrative form containing the title, brief prospectus, and committee chair.

The UHP form is not a substitute for the Full Thesis Proposal. The University Honors Program sets a baseline, while your department may require additional sections, approvals, or an oral presentation. Confirm both sources before you set your timeline.

Start with your major in the UHP Major and Thesis Requirements directory.

For an open program or curriculum question, use the official CFANS Directors of Undergraduate Studies (DUGS) directory. For an honors-specific question, contact the Honors Faculty Representative listed on your major’s UHP page or your Honors Advisor. The CFANS academic advising directory provides the current advising route.
Add the confirmed requirements to your working timeline.







ImportantDo Not Borrow Another Program’s Requirements



Do not infer a requirement from another department’s materials. If your own program does not publish the answer, mark it unconfirmed, record where you looked, and ask the appropriate program or honors contact. An honest open question is better than a false requirement.




Outreach Protocol
A generic message asking “can I do research with you?” gives the recipient little information for deciding how to respond. A useful first-contact message names a specific connection and makes a concrete request. Three paragraphs, under 200 words:

Who you are. Name, major, year, and that you are developing an honors thesis proposal in CFAN 3091V this semester.
Why them. Name the specific paper, project, or course you found before class, and explain its connection to the focused problem you funneled on Monday.
What you are asking for. A 20-minute conversation, with two or three times you are available.

The Advisor FAQ explains the course and includes a complete example message. Use its structure, but replace every bracketed field and generic phrase with details specific to you and the recipient.
Draft the strongest of the three messages in class. Then trade with a partner and test one thing: could this message have been sent to any faculty member in the college? If yes, paragraph two is not doing its work. Revise that message, then use it as a structural model when you complete the other two before your deadline on Friday, September 18.
Before you leave Wednesday, hand in the completed Requirements and Outreach worksheet. I will read it and return brief feedback. This is an in-class participation check based on the work you submit, not on attendance alone. Satisfactory work records the requirements search, analyzes three candidates, includes one complete message draft, and documents the peer test.
Complete the other two message drafts by Friday, September 18. Send all three messages no later than Monday, September 21. Keep dated copies for the Week 4 milestone fallback.
Bring the sent messages and any replies to your Week 3 meeting. We can revise the next action there, but the meeting is not the release point. This schedule leaves the five-business-day follow-up window intact before the Week 4 milestone.

Week 4: Literature Search and Source Evaluation
text:
Purpose
A large result count is not a literature base. It is only a result count. The work this week is to make the path inspectable: what you searched, where you searched, what changed, why a source stayed, and how one useful source led to another.






ImportantBring a Laptop This Week



Week 4 is the course’s screen-based exception because databases and Zotero are the subject of the instruction. Both sessions require a laptop and charger.
If you do not have a suitable device or cannot install Zotero, tell me before Monday. We will arrange an accessible course device or a browser-based fallback before class begins. Do not spend the workshop fighting an access problem in silence.

title: Week 4: Literature Search and Source Evaluation
section: Monday: Build a Search You Can Explain
text:
Monday: Build a Search You Can Explain
Format: Short demonstrations followed by guided work in your own field.



Table 1: Monday search-workshop outputs.









Segment
What you will produce




Question to concepts
Two to four concept groups drawn from your current question


Database choice
One starting database or disciplinary collection and a reason for choosing it


Query trial
A first query with the exact terms, limits, and result count recorded


Revision
At least one changed query and a sentence explaining the change


Source inspection
Two retained sources with a stated role and fit decision


Zotero setup
A thesis collection, course tags, verified item metadata, and one structured note






Use the Week 4 Search Workbook throughout the session. This is working documentation, not a polished product.

1. Move from a Question to Concepts
Most of you have never run a search in a library database, and a good number of you have never taken a logic course. You are not supposed to know this yet. That is why we are spending a full session on it, on paper first and at the keyboard second.
A database does not read your question. It matches the strings you hand it against the fields it has indexed. So the first move is not typing. It is taking the question apart.
Copy your current question or focused problem. Underline the parts that a database could index: a population or system, a process or exposure, an outcome, a place, a period, a method, or a type of source. Not every project needs the same categories.






TipBreakout: Where Keywords Actually Come From



You do not invent keywords. You harvest them from work that already exists, which is why we start from a paper you have already read rather than from a blank page.
Five places to harvest, in the order they usually pay off:

The title. Authors compress their topic into about a dozen words. Those words are load-bearing.
The abstract. Read it for nouns, not for argument. The population, the thing done, and the thing measured are usually all there.
The author keywords. Printed under the abstract in most journals. These are the terms the authors expect searchers to use.
The subject headings or descriptors. Assigned by the database, not the author, and visible on the record page. One good record hands you the controlled vocabulary of an entire field.
The introduction’s framing sentences. The terms an author uses to say what is already known are the terms already circulating in that literature.

A caution about the fourth item. Subject headings are powerful precisely because they are standardized, and standardization is field-specific. Health databases and agriculture databases can index the same study under different headings. Harvest from the database you are actually in.








TipBreakout: AND, OR, and NOT Before They Are Search Syntax



Forget databases for a minute. These three words are about sets: collections of things.
Picture every student in this room. Now picture two overlapping groups: the ones who have declared a major in the college, and the ones graduating in December.

OR is the union. “In the college OR graduating in December” gathers everyone in either group. Every person from both circles. OR makes the result larger.
AND is the intersection. “In the college AND graduating in December” keeps only the people in both groups at once. AND makes the result smaller.
NOT is exclusion. “In the college NOT graduating in December” keeps the first group and removes anyone who is also in the second.

Here is the part that trips people, every year, in every field. OR feels restrictive because the English word “or” often means “one or the other, pick one.” In a search it means “either counts, give me both.” AND feels generous because “and” sounds additive. In a search it is the strict one: every term you add with AND is another condition a record must satisfy simultaneously, and each one throws results away.
So the shape of a working search is: OR inside a concept, AND between concepts.
(cover crop OR "green manure" OR rye)    <- concept 1: synonyms, joined by OR
AND
(weed OR "weed suppression")             <- concept 2: synonyms, joined by OR
Alternate terms for one idea go inside one set of parentheses joined by OR, because any of them would be an acceptable hit. Different ideas are joined by AND, because a useful record has to be about both. The parentheses are not decoration. Without them the database applies the operators in its own default order and you get a result set you cannot explain.
Two mechanical notes that cause more failed searches than any concept: quotation marks hold a phrase together, so "cover crop" searches the phrase and cover crop may search the two words separately; and a truncation symbol, usually *, catches word endings, so weed* retrieves weed, weeds, and weedy. Both are conveniences with a cost. * placed too early, as in wee*, will hand you week, weekly, and weep.
Use NOT sparingly. It removes records permanently from your result set, including the ones that mention your unwanted term once, in passing, while being exactly what you needed.




Worked Exercise: Build a Keyword Table from the Davis Paper
We do this one together at the board before you do it on your own question. Use the paper you already dissected in Week 1, because you know what is in it and can spend the time on the method instead of on the reading.
Davis, A. S. (2010). Cover-crop roller-crimper contributes to weed management in no-till soybean. Weed Science, 58(3), 300-309.
Step one: pull the indexable ideas out of that title. There are roughly four. A practice, a machine, an outcome, and a crop system.
Step two: for each, list the other words a different field, decade, or country might use for the same idea. This is the step students skip, and it is the step that decides whether your search finds the literature or a slice of it.



Table 2: A keyword table built by harvesting one known paper. Each row is one idea; each row’s terms are joined by OR, and the rows are joined by AND.









Concept
Terms that mean roughly the same thing




Cover crop
cover crop, “green manure”, “living mulch”, rye, vetch


Roller-crimper
“roller crimper”, roller-crimper, “mechanical termination”


Weed outcome
weed, “weed suppression”, “weed management”, “weed density”


System
“no-till”, “no till”, conservation tillage, soybean






Notice three things about that table. Hyphens and spaces vary, so you search both forms. One row is a crop and one row is a tillage system, which means the “System” row may need to become two rows once you see how it behaves. And “rye” is in the first row even though it is a species rather than a synonym, because in this literature a rye search retrieves cover-crop work that never uses the phrase “cover crop.”
Step three: keep the table. This is your keyword database, and it is a living document. Every time a good record shows you a term you did not have, add it to the right row and note where you found it. By Week 5 the table is part of the evidence that your search was systematic rather than lucky.
Now build the same table for your own question in the Search Workbook. Four rows at most. If you cannot fill a row with at least two alternate terms, that is worth saying out loud in class: either the concept is already precise, or you do not yet know the vocabulary of the literature you are entering.
Database syntax varies, so record the exact version you actually ran rather than pretending one string works everywhere.


2. Choose the Search Environment
Choose by coverage, not by habit. A database is not a neutral window onto the literature. It is a bounded collection that somebody decided to build, and the boundary is the whole point: what a database does not index, you will not find in it, no matter how good your search string is.
That gives you a rule you can apply without knowing anything about a specific database. Ask what a collection was built to cover, then ask whether your question lives inside that coverage.
There are three kinds of tool in play this week, and they do different jobs.



Table 3: What each kind of search tool is built for. Match the tool to the question rather than to habit.










Kind of tool
What it is built to do
What it costs you




Multidisciplinary index, such as Web of Science or Scopus
Spans many fields and supports citation tracing in both directions
Breadth means less field-specific indexing, so the controlled vocabulary is thinner


Subject database, such as PubMed for health and life sciences
Deep coverage and specialist subject headings for one domain
A question that straddles domains falls partly outside the boundary


Web search engine, such as Google Scholar
Retrieves a known item fast and follows cited-by links
Coverage and ranking are undisclosed, so a search cannot be described or reproduced






Policy, economics, history, design, education, and qualitative work each have their own subject collections, and your project may need one this table does not name.






ImportantThe Two Library Routes Worth Your Time



The University Libraries help and research-guide routes are how you find out which collection covers your question. Two things there are worth more than the rest, so use these rather than browsing.
Research guides. A subject librarian has already written down which databases cover a field and which are the starting points. That is exactly the question you are trying to answer, answered by someone who does it professionally. Reading the guide for your field takes about 10 minutes and routinely saves an hour of guessing.
A research consultation. You can meet with a librarian about your specific question. This is a free, ordinary service that graduate students use constantly, and undergraduates underuse. Bring your keyword table and your decision log; a consultation with a documented failed search is far more productive than one that starts with “I need sources.”
Access runs through your University login, so a paywall you hit off-campus is usually a login problem rather than a real barrier. If a database asks for payment, stop and route it through the Libraries instead of paying.


Google Scholar deserves a specific warning rather than a general one. It is genuinely useful for retrieving a title you already know and for following a cited-by link. But it does not publish what it indexes or how it ranks, which means you cannot state its coverage, cannot reproduce today’s result set tomorrow, and cannot defend the boundary of your search. Use it as a supplement to a search you can describe, not as the search itself.


3. Keep a Decision Log
Run the first query, then inspect the result set before changing anything. Record:

the database and date;
the exact query and filters;
the result count;
two results that fit and one that does not; and
the single change you will make next.

If a query fails, keep it. A failed query with a diagnosed problem is evidence of a decision. A perfect-looking final string with no path into it is not.

This Is the Second Half of the Ledger You Started in Week 1
Recall from Week 1 that we filled in the Literature Intake Form together on the Davis paper, and that its last section had you write a first claims-and-evidence entry: the claim, the evidence and its location, why the evidence is relevant, a limit, and a status. That was not a one-week exercise. It was the first row of a record you keep all semester.
You are now building the other half of that record, and the two answer different questions:



Table 4: The two records and the different questions each one answers. Together they make a source set inspectable from discovery through use.










Record
Question it answers
Started




Search decision log
How did I find this, and what did I look at and reject on the way?
This week


Claims-and-evidence ledger
What may I actually use from this source, on what evidence, and within what limits?
Week 1






Neither one substitutes for the other. A search log with no ledger tells a reader you looked, but not what you found that you can stand behind. A ledger with no search log tells a reader what you believe, but not whether you looked anywhere you might have been contradicted.
The connection is operational, not just conceptual. When a source survives the role and fit decision in step four, it does not stop at the search log. Open a ledger entry for it using the same five fields you used in Week 1. Then the citation key in your log and the citation key in your ledger are the same string, and you can move between the two records without reconstructing anything.
The forms are on the course site and stay available all semester:

Week 1 Literature Intake Form, including the printable two-page version, for the five ledger fields; and
the reading protocol for the longer procedure behind a careful entry.

Week 1 also described how to move these entries off paper once the structure is habit: fixed-heading child notes in Zotero, one row per claim in a spreadsheet, or linked source and claim tables in a database. Week 4 is a reasonable point to make that move, because this is the week your source count starts growing faster than your memory. One warning from that discussion is worth repeating now that you have Zotero open: keep one row per claim, not one row per article. A single paper routinely supports three usable claims and undercuts a fourth.



4. Evaluate Role and Fit
Do not ask only whether a source is peer reviewed. Ask what work it can do for this project.



Table 5: Source-role and fit decisions for the first inspection.









Decision
Questions to ask




Source role
Is this a primary study, review, methods source, policy or technical report, dataset, or other gray literature?


Question fit
Which part of my question does it address, and which part does it not address?


Evidence fit
Do the data, sources, cases, or methods support the claim I want to use?


Context
Is the population, system, place, or period close enough for the intended use?


Currency
Does this claim require current information, or is the source foundational?


Traceability
Can I identify the author, venue or issuing body, date, and evidence path?






The outcome is not a universal score. It is a bounded decision: keep for a named purpose, set aside with a reason, or inspect more closely before using.


5. Build a Zotero Library That Preserves Decisions
The University Libraries citation-management page and Zotero documentation provide current installation and troubleshooting guidance. In class:

Create one collection for the thesis project.
Save sources from the item page when possible, not from an isolated PDF.
Check the item type, title, authors, year, journal or publisher, volume, issue, pages, and Digital Object Identifier (DOI) after capture.
Use the tags pearl, backward, and forward for discovery path. Add core, supporting, or background only after deciding the source’s role.
Attach a note with three headings: Main contribution, Connection to my question, and Limits or unresolved questions.

Zotero stores what you give it. A captured record with bad metadata produces a bad citation faster. Verify first.

title: Week 4: Literature Search and Source Evaluation
text:
Wednesday: Grow a Source Set
Format: Reading clinic, citation-network workshop, and partner audit.

Reading Clinic: Who Does This Paper Cite?
Bring your marked Week 1 article and the reading protocol. Choose two or three framing sentences in the introduction. For each sentence, identify the source or sources cited and name the job the citation is doing: defining the problem, establishing what is known, marking a disagreement, or justifying the study.
This manual trace is the bridge into pearl growing. You are not collecting every citation. You are following the ones that do work relevant to your question.


Pearl-Growing Workflow

Choose the pearl. Find one review article published in 2020 or later that is close enough to orient your problem. If no suitable review exists, document the search and use a well-connected primary or methods source after checking with me.
Trace backward. Select five cited sources that bear directly on your focused problem. Record the reason for each selection. Repeated citation is a clue, not an automatic inclusion rule.
Trace forward. Use a cited-by tool in Web of Science, Scopus, or Google Scholar. Select five later sources that cite the pearl and address your problem. Record the reason for each selection.
Capture and verify. Add the pearl and the 10 traced sources to Zotero. Apply the discovery-path tags and correct incomplete metadata.
Annotate three. For one pearl, backward, and forward source, record the main contribution, connection to your question, and limits or unresolved questions.
Audit with a partner. Ask whether another reader can reconstruct why each of the three annotated sources belongs in the set.

If a branch produces nothing useful, record that result. Change the pearl, move one concept level broader, or take the documented question to a University Libraries research consultation.

title: Week 1 Literature Intake
Reading Protocol
text: Use this as a starting procedure when the course puts an empirical research paper in front of you. Keep it with your drafts and mark up the article in a format you can use. The procedure is a heuristic, not a universal map. Some disciplines use recognizable introduction, methods, results, and discussion sections. Others organize questions, arguments, observations, themes, cases, or models differently.

title: Reading Protocol
section: Do Not Read It Front to Back
text:
Do Not Read It Front to Back
The first instinct may be to start at the first word and read to the last one. For many empirical papers, a targeted first pass makes the structure visible before you read closely.
Read in this order instead.



Table 1: Reading order for a first pass through a research article.










Order
Where you go
What you are after




1
Title and abstract
The claim, in the authors’ most confident phrasing


2
Last paragraph of the introduction
The actual question, and usually the hypothesis


3
Results, findings, evidence displays, or key passages
The evidence connected to the claim


4
First and last paragraphs of the discussion
What the authors say the evidence means


5
Methods
How the evidence was produced, read only as closely as you need


6
The rest, if you still need it
Detail






The time required depends on the paper, the discipline, and your purpose. A targeted pass helps you decide where closer reading is needed.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
The Four Questions
For any paper, on any pass, you are answering these. Write the answers in the margins.

What question were the authors trying to answer? State it as a question, in your own words, in one sentence.
What did they conclude? Find the sentence in the paper that says it. Underline it. Do not paraphrase yet.
What evidence is that conclusion resting on? Point at the specific result, observation, estimate, figure, table, quotation, theme, case, model, passage, or other form of evidence. If you cannot find one, that is a finding.
Where are the seams? Mark where each section starts and name the job it is doing.

Question 3 is where the most useful work begins. If the connection is not immediately visible, you have found something worth investigating, not made a mistake. Question 2 gives you the authors’ conclusion. Question 3 asks what is holding that conclusion up. Learning to trace the connection between the two is a skill, and each careful attempt strengthens it.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
What Each Section Is Doing
Many empirical research articles and proposals contain the parts below, even when the labels, order, or boundaries differ. Once you can see the work each part is doing, you can compare that structure with other disciplinary forms and with your own draft.



Table 2: What each section of a research article is doing.










Section
The job it does
What to look for




Abstract
Sells the paper in 250 words
The strongest version of the claim


Introduction
Narrows from a field to one unanswered question
Where the funnel lands, in the last paragraph


Literature review
Argues that a specific gap exists
Whether it synthesizes or just lists


Methods
Lets a stranger repeat the study
What was measured, on how many units, compared with what


Results or findings
Reports what was found, sometimes with interpretation
Results, observations, themes, estimates, uncertainty, and the evidence available for each claim


Discussion
Interprets, connects, and concedes
Where interpretation outruns the results


Conclusion
Says what it adds and what comes next
Whether the claim has quietly grown


References
Shows whose conversation this is
Names that keep recurring






Two of these are worth flagging now. Results and discussion are different jobs, even when a discipline combines them in one section. Watch how the authors move from reporting evidence to interpreting it. You will need to make that move visible in your own work later in the semester.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
The Second Pass
Everything above is structural. It tells you what a paper says. It does not tell you whether to believe it.
The evaluative pass comes in Week 6, where you take each claim and ask how many were studied, how large the effect was, and what the figures are not showing. Do not try to run both passes at once early in the semester. Find the parts first. Judge them second.

title: Reading Protocol
text:
Common Traps

Looking up every unfamiliar term. On a first pass, keep going. Circle the terms and come back. Stopping at each one means you never see the shape.
Trusting the abstract. The abstract is the most confident and least qualified text in the paper. Check it against the results.
Reading the methods first and getting stuck. Methods sections are dense by design. They are step 5 for a reason.
Taking notes instead of marking up. Notes drift into summary. Marking up keeps you anchored to what the paper actually says.
Treating a paper as settled. A published paper is one contribution to an argument that is still running, not the final word on it.

When You Read for Your Own Project
Add one question to the four above: what does this change about my question? Record the answer in your source notes while it is fresh. That running record is what makes the synthesis matrix in Week 8 possible, and it is part of your process portfolio.

Two of these reports are the agenda for your individual meeting with me. title: Progress Reports
text:
The Template
Every report answers the same four questions. Keep it to one page. This is not an essay, and length is not the point.
1. What did you accomplish since the last report?
Be specific. Dates, meetings, hours, sources added, words drafted, analyses run. “I worked on my literature review” tells me nothing. “I added nine sources to Zotero, read four of them closely, and drafted two paragraphs on the nitrogen-timing disagreement” tells me where you are.
2. What did you struggle with, and how did you try to resolve it?
The second half of that question matters as much as the first. Naming an obstacle is useful. Naming what you already tried tells me whether you need a different approach or just more time, and it keeps me from suggesting the thing you did last Tuesday.
3. What is your plan for the next period?
Specific tasks with specific deadlines. “Keep reading” is not a plan. “Finish the three forward-citation papers by Oct 12 and draft the methods paragraph by Oct 15” is a plan, and it gives us something to check against next time.
4. What questions do you have for me?
Bring them written down. The questions you think of in the moment are rarely the ones that have been slowing you down for two weeks.

title: Progress Reports
text:
What “Satisfactory” Means
Progress reports are a completion check-in. I read them; I do not give line-level feedback on them. See the feedback tiers.
A report is satisfactory when it:

answers all four questions;
is specific enough that someone could act on it, with named tasks, sources, dates, or obstacles rather than general statements of effort;
is submitted before the deadline, which for meeting weeks means before your meeting time, not after it; and
describes the work honestly, including the parts that did not go well.

A report is not yet satisfactory when it is missing a question, is written at a level of generality that could describe any student in any week, or arrives after the meeting it was supposed to structure.






NoteA Report Saying “I Am Stuck” Is Satisfactory



Satisfactory describes the report, not the project. A week where you accomplished little, struggled with something you could not resolve, and have questions you cannot answer yourself is a completely normal week in thesis work. Write that down without dressing it up and the report is satisfactory. What is not satisfactory is concealing it, because then I cannot help and we both discover the problem in November.

title: Assignments Overview
text:
Major Deliverables

Full Thesis Proposal (Course Assignment)
This is the substantial document you develop and submit for CFAN 3091V. It is not the same thing as the shorter UHP Thesis Proposal Form. The complete proposal includes the sections required by your program. At minimum, the working course structure includes:

title and project identification;
introduction and research question;
literature review;
proposed methods;
expected results and alternative outcomes;
discussion of significance and limitations;
figures or tables when appropriate; and
references.

Program-specific requirements take precedence over this working list.


Final Thesis Draft (Fall Graduation Track)
Students graduating in Fall 2026 submit a complete thesis rather than a new proposal. The thesis must reflect the Primary Advisor and Proposal Committee review, meet applicable program requirements, and be filed with the UHP Thesis Completion Form by December 14, 2026. On December 16, students submit the process portfolio and the completion-submission record to the course. Committee approval remains an institutional decision, not a course grade assigned by the instructor.


UHP Thesis Proposal Form (University Requirement)
This is a separate, shorter administrative submission through the Honors Reporting Center. It asks for your thesis title, a brief prospectus, and your committee chair. For spring or summer graduates, the current PDF lists a December 1 deadline; fall graduates have a June 30 deadline. Confirm the current date and any earlier department deadline with your advisor. The Week 13 instructor conversation does not replace this filing.


Foundations Milestones
The Weeks 1-4 milestones move from the course-track survey and an interest and direction freewrite through topic narrowing and faculty identification to a primary-advisor plan. See Foundations Milestones, which also covers what to submit if no faculty member has agreed by Sep 30.


Progress Reports
Short structured accounts of where the project stands. Two of them serve as your individual-meeting agenda. See the Progress Reports page for the template, the standard, and the Professional Review Plan.


Written Assignments
Four milestones contain the course’s main writing assignments: the Week 2 writing exercise and topic funnel, the Method and Feasibility Blueprint, the Literature Synthesis Draft, and the Introduction, Literature Review, and Methods Draft. Milestone 2 also includes the separate Requirements and Outreach participation worksheet. The writing assignments escalate, and each produces material the next one uses. See the Written Assignments page.


The Document
Your proposal or thesis passes three checkpoints: advisor-ready and released after the Week 12 screen, discussed with the instructor and confirmed in professional review in Week 13, and final in Week 15. The Fall Graduation thesis is due Dec 14; the Proposal Development document is due Dec 16. See The Document.


Process Portfolio
The portfolio documents development across searching, reading, writing, feedback, revision, mentor communication, and proposal or thesis decisions. See the Process Portfolio page.


Instructor Conversation and Release Checkpoint
The Week 13 conversation asks you to explain the proposal or thesis, respond to questions about evidence and design, and identify the revisions required before the document is sent to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee.


Peer Reviews
Two structured student peer reviews focus on the reader’s experience, the evidence in the draft, and the writer’s stated goals. See the Peer Review Guidelines.


Professional Review
After the Week 12 release screen, send the revised document to the Primary Advisor and/or Proposal Committee. Week 13 confirms that the document was sent and uses the instructor conversation to sharpen the review questions. Submit evidence of professional review, a response memo, and a prioritized revision plan in Week 14. You are assessed on preparation, professional communication, and your use of feedback, not on how quickly another person responds.
If no substantive response has arrived by Dec 9, a documented send, a follow-up message, a self-review against the reviewer criteria, and a prioritized revision plan satisfy the milestone in full. A dated, redacted record and your own summary are sufficient; raw email threads and private reviewer information are not required. See Week 14 for what to submit. Tell the instructor during the week rather than on Dec 9.

title: Week 8: Literature Synthesis Draft
text:
What This Assignment Is
This is the first substantive draft in the course and the first assignment that receives detailed written feedback. The Monday workshop builds the matrix. The independent Wednesday work turns that matrix into a literature synthesis that does more than summarize sources one at a time.
A literature review is not a sequence of article summaries. It is an argument about what is known, how it is known, where findings converge, and what remains uncertain. The synthesis matrix built on Monday is the tool; this draft is the result.
The Week 8 module explains the three moves the draft has to make and the four jobs a sentence in it can do.

text:

title: Week 8: Literature Synthesis Draft
Week 8: Literature Synthesis Draft
text:
The Failure Mode to Avoid
This is where drafts most often fail: they summarize sources without linking them back to the question they are supposed to sharpen.
“No one has studied this” is almost never true and is easy for a committee to disprove. “These studies address X in system A, but not in system B, where the mechanism may differ” is defensible.
